faqs.question: What does AI warehouse robotics actually automate?
faqs.answer: Autonomous item transport between warehouse zones, robotic picking for standard-shape inventory, continuous inventory location optimization, and coordination across multiple robots operating in the same physical space.

faqs.question: How is warehouse robotics different from logistics software?
faqs.answer: Warehouse robotics is the physical-execution layer inside a facility, robots that move and pick inventory. Logistics software like route optimization and order fulfillment automation operates around that physical step, planning what happens before and after, not the physical movement itself.

faqs.question: Can robots pick any item in a warehouse?
faqs.answer: Not reliably. Robotic picking works well for inventory with predictable shape and packaging. Irregular, fragile, or damaged items still need a person to handle the physical exception safely.

faqs.question: Is warehouse robotics safe to operate alongside human workers?
faqs.answer: It can be, but safety protocol design and enforcement in a shared robot-and-human workspace is a genuine human responsibility that requires deliberate engineering, not something to assume the robotic system's sensors handle completely on their own.

faqs.question: Does AI warehouse robotics eliminate the need for warehouse staff?
faqs.answer: No. It shifts staff time away from routine transport and picking toward exception handling, facility oversight, and safety management, work that still requires people physically present and capable of taking over if a robotic system fails.

faqs.question: What should a warehouse operator evaluate before adopting robotics?
faqs.answer:
Facility layout compatibility, the proportion of inventory that fits standard picking parameters, safety protocol requirements for shared human-robot space, and a realistic plan for handling equipment failure or facility disruption without stopping operations.

/blog/anthropic-conway-claude-always-on-.title: Anthropic Conway: Inside Claude's Always-On Agent Platform (2026)
/blog/anthropic-conway-claude-always-on-.description: Anthropic is secretly testing Conway, an always-on AI agent for Claude with browser control, webhooks, and a CNW extension ecosystem.

faqs.question: What is Anthropic Conway?
faqs.answer: Anthropic Conway is a persistent, always-on AI agent platform built on top of Claude. Unlike standard Claude chat sessions, Conway operates continuously in the background, can be triggered by external webhooks, controls a browser directly, and supports a custom extension ecosystem via the CNW ZIP standard.

faqs.question: How is Conway different from Claude.ai?
faqs.answer: Claude.ai is a conversational interface where Claude responds to user prompts within a session. Conway is a persistent agent environment that runs whether or not you are actively using it. It can initiate actions based on external events, complete long-horizon tasks autonomously, and send notifications when it needs input or has completed a task.

faqs.question: What is the CNW ZIP extension standard?
faqs.answer: CNW ZIP is Anthropic's upcoming extension format for the Conway platform. Developers can package custom tools, UI tabs, and context handlers into .cnw.zip files that install directly into a Conway instance. This creates an app-store-style ecosystem for extending Conway's capabilities with specialized integrations.

faqs.question: Can Conway control a browser?
faqs.answer: Yes. Based on leaked interface details, Conway has native browser control capabilities. It can navigate pages, fill forms, extract data, and complete multi-step workflows that require UI interaction. This is similar to Claude Computer Use but integrated into the persistent agent environment.

faqs.question: How does Conway use webhooks?
faqs.answer: Conway can be invoked by external services sending HTTP webhook requests to a Conway endpoint. This means any event-driven system: CRM updates, CI/CD pipeline events, messaging platforms, or databases, can trigger autonomous Conway workflows without a human initiating a prompt.

faqs.question: When will Anthropic Conway be publicly available?
faqs.answer: Anthropic has not announced a public release date for Conway. As of April 2026, the platform is in limited internal testing. Given the complexity of safety and governance requirements for always-on agents, a broader rollout is likely months away.

faqs.question: What is the difference between Conway and Claude Code?
faqs.answer: Claude Code is Anthropic's agentic coding assistant that developers run manually in their terminal or IDE. Conway is a persistent background agent that can invoke Claude Code as a sub-agent within larger automated workflows. Conway adds always-on operation, webhook triggers, browser control, and the extension ecosystem on top of Claude Code's coding capabilities.

faqs.question: What security risks does an always-on agent like Conway introduce?
faqs.answer: A persistent agent with browser access, code execution, and external connectivity introduces significant risks including unauthorized data access, prompt injection via connected services, and supply chain risks in the extension ecosystem. Enterprise deployments will require defined permission scopes, audit logging, and clear escalation policies. Our AI agent development team advises on secure agent architecture for exactly these scenarios.

faqs.question: How does Conway compare to OpenAI's Operator?
faqs.answer: OpenAI's Operator also supports browser control but operates as a single-session tool rather than a persistent background agent. Conway adds always-on operation, webhook triggers, and an open extension standard that Operator does not currently offer. Conway is currently in testing; Operator has had limited public availability since early 2025.

faqs.question: Can businesses build on Conway today?
faqs.answer:
Not publicly. Conway is not yet available via API or as a developer platform. However, businesses can prepare by auditing which workflows are candidates for agent delegation, mapping event-driven triggers in their existing systems, and evaluating custom workflow automation frameworks that will integrate with Conway when it ships.

/blog/best-ai-agent-observability-tools.title: 12 Best AI Agent Observability Tools in 2026 (Tracing, Evals, Cost Tracking)
/blog/best-ai-agent-observability-tools.description: 12 AI agent observability tools compared on tracing, evals, token cost tracking and self-hosting. Covers Langfuse, Opik, Arize Phoenix, Helicone, LangSmith, Datadog and six more, with a guide to picking by situation.

faqs.question: What is the difference between LLM observability and AI agent observability?
faqs.answer: LLM observability tracks individual model calls, while AI agent observability tracks full multi-step runs. Agents chain planning calls, tool calls, and retrieval, so agent observability captures the whole trace and the relationships between steps, not one prompt and completion alone.

faqs.question: Which AI agent observability tool is best for cost tracking?
faqs.answer: Helicone is the strongest pure cost-tracking option because its proxy model captures every request automatically and prices 300-plus models precisely. Langfuse and OpenLIT also track cost well if you prefer a self-hosted, full-platform approach.

faqs.question: Are open-source observability tools good enough for production?
faqs.answer: Yes. Langfuse, Arize Phoenix, and OpenLIT all run in production at scale and offer tracing, evals, and cost tracking. Open-source tools give you data ownership and no per-seat lock-in, at the cost of running and maintaining the infrastructure yourself.

faqs.question: What is the best open-source AI agent observability tool?
faqs.answer: Langfuse is the broadest all-in-one open-source option, with an MIT core covering tracing, prompts and evals. Opik (Apache 2.0) fits if you want 30-plus built-in eval metrics and guardrails. Arize Phoenix fits RAG-heavy work and runs locally with no account. All three are free to self-host.

faqs.question: Which observability tool works best for CrewAI or multi-agent systems?
faqs.answer: AgentOps is built around agent sessions, with native integrations for CrewAI, AG2 (AutoGen), LangGraph and the OpenAI Agents SDK, plus step-by-step replay of each run. If you also need deep evals next to the traces, Opik lists CrewAI and AutoGen among its 60-plus framework integrations.

faqs.question: How much do AI agent observability tools cost?
faqs.answer: Several start free. Pydantic Logfire includes 10 million records a month free, then Team costs $49 a month. AgentOps is free up to 5,000 events a month, with Pro from $40 a month. Langfuse, Phoenix, Opik and OpenLIT are free to self-host, so your main cost is infrastructure. Prices checked September 26, 2026.

faqs.question: Do I need OpenTelemetry for AI agent observability?
faqs.answer: You do not strictly need it, but it helps. OpenTelemetry is a vendor-neutral standard, so instrumenting with it (often through OpenLLMetry or OpenInference) lets you switch or combine backends without re-instrumenting your code. Most leading tools in 2026 support it.

faqs.question: What are evals in the context of agent observability?
faqs.answer: Evals are automated scores that measure output quality against a dataset or an LLM-as-judge rubric. You run them offline before shipping to catch regressions and online in production to monitor live quality. Braintrust and LangSmith offer the deepest eval workflows.

faqs.question: Can I use more than one observability tool together?
faqs.answer: Yes, and many teams do. A common setup pairs an OpenTelemetry instrumentation layer like Traceloop OpenLLMetry with a backend such as Langfuse or Datadog, then adds Helicone as a proxy for precise cost attribution. The standards-based approach makes combining tools straightforward.

faqs.question: How much engineering effort does it take to add observability?
faqs.answer:
It ranges from one line to a short integration. Proxy tools like Helicone and auto-instrumenting platforms like OpenLIT need almost no code. SDK-based platforms like Langfuse, Phoenix, and Braintrust take a bit more setup but give you finer control over what you capture.

For the Claude API integration that most of these tools observe, the Claude Fable 5 API tutorial covers streaming, tool use, and prompt caching setup.

faqs.question: What are generative AI consulting services?
faqs.answer: Generative AI consulting services cover strategic advisory, use-case identification, solution design, and deployment planning for large language model-based systems, distinct from broader AI/ML consulting or workflow automation. Big 4 firms and MBB consultancies both offer generative AI consulting services as a named practice area. No published rate card; pricing is quoted per engagement.

faqs.question: How much does an AI automation consultant cost?
faqs.answer: Most firms on this list publish no rate card, and pricing is quoted per engagement. The one public hourly range here is LeewayHertz on Clutch: $50 to $99 per hour with a $10,000+ minimum project (checked 2026-09-26). For comparison, a full-time CAIO runs $250,000 or more a year, and ManasFlow scopes a fractional retainer after a strategy audit.

faqs.question: What is the difference between an AI consultant and an AI automation agency?
faqs.answer: A consultant is hired primarily for advice: strategy, architecture, and governance recommendations. An agency is hired to build and run the automation itself. Many buyers need both, which is why several firms on this list, including ManasFlow, LeewayHertz, Kanerika, Neurons Lab, Vstorm, Addepto and deepsense.ai, offer strategy and build under one roof rather than requiring a separate implementation vendor.

faqs.question: Do I need a fractional CAIO or a full-time Chief AI Officer?
faqs.answer: A full-time CAIO makes sense once AI is a majority of your product or operating strategy and you can justify $250,000 or more a year before benefits and equity. A fractional CAIO gives mid-sized organizations the same strategic ownership on a retainer scoped to the engagement, for teams not yet ready for that full-time commitment.

faqs.question: Should I hire a Big 4 firm or a boutique AI consultant?
faqs.answer: Big 4 and MBB firms bring board-level credibility, global delivery scale, and deep regulated-industry experience, priced by proposal with no published rate card. Boutique consultants and fractional models work at mid-market budgets, but with a smaller delivery bench. If you need a multi-region, multi-business-unit rollout, the scale firms are usually worth the premium. If you need one clear AI roadmap for a single organization, a boutique firm usually costs less to start. That difference in scale is why this guide lists the two groups separately instead of ranking them against each other.

faqs.question: What should I look for when evaluating an AI automation consultant?
faqs.answer: Focus on four things: (1) whether the firm's recommendations have historically made it into production, not just a strategy deck, (2) technical depth in your specific AI capabilities (agents, RAG, workflow orchestration, data infrastructure), (3) transparency about what they can and can't verify publicly, and (4) whether their pricing model and company size actually match your budget and organization size. Ask for references and request a scoped first engagement before committing to a multi-year program.

faqs.question: Do AI automation consultants publish their rates?
faqs.answer: Few do. Neurons Lab, Vstorm, Addepto, Tribe AI and deepsense.ai publish no rates on their own sites, and the enterprise firms price by proposal. The only hourly figure in this guide comes from LeewayHertz's Clutch profile. ManasFlow publishes one number: engineer placement from $60,000 a year. Expect a scoping call before any quote.

faqs.question: What should the first engagement with an AI consultant deliver?
faqs.answer: A ranked list of use cases with cost and benefit estimates, and ideally a working proof of concept on your own data. Addepto lists both as deliverables. ManasFlow's strategy audit covers use cases, data readiness, risks, team capability, implementation effort and expected value. A slide deck of generic AI trends is a warning sign.

faqs.question: What is a forward-deployed AI engineer?
faqs.answer: A forward-deployed engineer works inside your team, on your systems, instead of building from the vendor's office and handing over a finished project. Tribe AI and Neurons Lab both describe this embedded way of working on their sites. ManasFlow offers a related model: an embedded AI engineer placed in 2 to 4 weeks, from $60,000 a year.

faqs.question: Should I hire an AI consultant that specializes in my industry?
faqs.answer:
It matters most in regulated sectors. A specialist such as Neurons Lab, which centers its offer on banks and insurers, already works with the compliance and accuracy rules you work under. For general workflow automation, industry depth matters less than whether the firm has shipped agents to production. Ask for a case study in your sector before signing.

faqs.question: What does an app development agency do?
faqs.answer: An app development agency designs, builds, and launches mobile or web apps for clients, and usually maintains them after launch. The work covers product scoping, UX and UI design, front-end and back-end engineering, App Store and Play Store submission, and ongoing updates. Agencies differ mainly in the build type they are set up for: fixed-timeline MVPs, premium design-led apps, or regulated enterprise builds.

faqs.question: How much does it cost to hire an app development agency?
faqs.answer: Costs on this list range from around $10,000 (Wve Labs) to $500,000+ for larger engagements (3 Sided Cube, Saritasa). ManasFlow's 30-day sprint and MindSea's healthcare builds are both scoped per project rather than a flat rate card. faqs.question: What is the difference between an app development agency and a software development agency?

"App development agency" usually implies the deliverable is a mobile or web application specifically, while "software development agency" can include backend systems, internal tools, or infrastructure with no consumer-facing app at all. faqs.question: Should I hire a generalist app agency or a vertical specialist?

ManasFlow specifically engineers AI agent and automation features as part of the same build rather than as a bolt-on requiring a second vendor. Ask any agency directly what AI capability they've actually shipped, not just discussed.

faqs.question: What should I ask before signing with an app development agency?
faqs.answer: Ask for a specific delivery date in the contract, not a range. Ask who owns the codebase, app-store accounts, and any third-party API keys after handoff. Ask for a past app that's still live and maintained today, not just a portfolio screenshot. If your build has a specific vertical requirement, ask for a named, checkable example in that exact space.

faqs.question: What are Claude Code slash commands?
faqs.answer: Slash commands are built-in shortcuts you type directly into the Claude Code terminal. They start with a forward slash (like /init or /review) and trigger specific functionality without needing to write a full natural language prompt. They are faster and more reliable than asking Claude to perform the same action through a regular message.

faqs.question: How do I see all available Claude Code commands?
faqs.answer: Type / in the Claude Code terminal and you will see an autocomplete list of all available commands, including both built-in commands and any custom skills you have created. You can also type /help for a summary of the most important commands and what they do.

faqs.question: Is /compact the same as /clear?
faqs.answer: No. /compact compresses your conversation into a summary while preserving the key context and decisions. /clear erases everything and starts from scratch. Use /compact when you want to keep working on the same task with a lighter context. Use /clear when you are switching to something completely unrelated.

faqs.question: How much does a Claude Code session cost?
faqs.answer: Costs vary based on the model and how many tokens you use. The /cost command shows your exact usage for the current session. A typical 30-minute coding session might use 500K to 2M tokens depending on how many files Claude reads and how much code it generates. Using /compact regularly helps keep costs down by reducing redundant context in each message.

faqs.question: Can I share custom slash commands with my team?
faqs.answer: Yes. Custom skills are markdown files stored in .claude/skills/ within your project directory. Commit this directory to version control and every team member who clones the repo gets the same custom commands. This is the recommended way to standardize Claude Code workflows across a team.

faqs.question: Do slash commands work with all Claude models?
faqs.answer: Yes. Slash commands are part of the Claude Code client, not the underlying model. They work regardless of which Claude model you are using. The commands themselves execute on the client side and then send the appropriate prompts or actions to whichever model is active.

faqs.question: What is the difference between CLAUDE.md and memory files?
faqs.answer: CLAUDE.md is a project-level file typically generated by /init and checked into version control. It gives Claude context about your codebase structure, tech stack, and conventions. Memory files managed through /memory are personal or project-specific notes that persist across sessions. Think of CLAUDE.md as the team playbook and memory files as your personal notebook.

faqs.question: How do I create an MCP-powered custom command?
faqs.answer:
Custom skills can reference MCP tools in their instructions. If you have an MCP server configured (like a database connector or API integration), your skill's instructions can tell Claude to use those tools as part of the command workflow. For example, a skill could instruct Claude to query a Postgres database via an MCP server, analyze the results, and generate a report. The skill file itself is still just markdown with instructions. The MCP connection is configured separately in your Claude Code settings.

faqs.question: What are Claude Code hooks?
faqs.answer: Claude Code hooks are shell commands that execute automatically at specific points in Claude Code's lifecycle. They intercept tool calls (like file edits, bash commands, and commits), validate outputs, and enforce rules deterministically. Unlike prompt instructions, hooks run every time regardless of how you phrase your request.

faqs.question: Where do I configure Claude Code hooks?
faqs.answer: Hooks are configured in JSON settings files. Use ~/.claude/settings.json for global hooks that apply to all projects, or .claude/settings.json in your project root for project-specific hooks that can be shared with your team via version control.

faqs.question: What is the difference between PreToolUse and PostToolUse hooks?
faqs.answer: PreToolUse hooks fire before a tool executes and can block the action (exit code 2), allow it (exit code 0), or prompt for confirmation. PostToolUse hooks fire after a tool succeeds and cannot undo the action. Use PreToolUse for validation and gatekeeping, PostToolUse for formatting, testing, and notifications.

faqs.question: Can hooks slow down Claude Code?
faqs.answer: Yes. Every PreToolUse hook adds latency before each matching tool call. Keep hooks fast (under one second) and use specific matchers to avoid running hooks on irrelevant tools. If a hook involves network calls or heavy computation, consider moving it to PostToolUse or the Stop event instead.

faqs.question: How do I debug a hook that is not working?
faqs.answer: Test your hook script independently by piping sample JSON into it: echo '{"tool_input":{"command":"git commit -m test"},"cwd":"/tmp"}' | bash your-hook.sh. Check the exit code with echo $?. Exit code 0 means allow, 2 means block. Any stderr output is sent back to Claude as context.

faqs.question: What is document automation?
faqs.answer: Document automation is software that builds documents such as contracts, quotes, invoices, and statements of work from templates and live data, instead of someone copying values in by hand. Most tools add conditional clauses, approval routing, and an eSignature handoff on top of the template.

faqs.question: What is the best document automation software for Salesforce?
faqs.answer: DocuSign Gen for Salesforce and Conga Composer are the strongest picks for generating documents from Salesforce records, and S-Docs is the choice when every step has to stay native to Salesforce. DocuSign Gen starts at $20 per user per month and needs a separate eSignature plan.

faqs.question: Is there free document automation software?
faqs.answer: Yes, with limits. PandaDoc has a free eSign plan, S-Docs offers a limited free version on the Salesforce AppExchange, and DocuSign Gen has a 30-day free trial. Expect caps on templates or documents, so use a free tier to test one workflow before you buy.

faqs.question: What is the difference between document automation and intelligent document processing?
faqs.answer: Document automation creates outgoing documents from templates and data, while intelligent document processing (IDP) reads incoming documents such as invoices and contracts and extracts their data. Many teams need both: IDP to capture data from inbound paperwork and document automation to produce the contracts and quotes that go out.

faqs.question: How much does document automation software cost?
faqs.answer: Public prices start at $20 per user per month for DocuSign Gen for Salesforce (plus an eSignature plan), and Formstack's Suite bundle with Forms, Documents, and Sign costs $250 a month billed annually. Conga, Experlogix, HotDocs, Templafy, and Windward sell on custom quotes, and Microsoft's content assembly bills pay-as-you-go through Azure.

/blog/best-embedding-models.title: 12 Best Embedding Models for RAG and Semantic Search (2026 Benchmarks and Pricing)
/blog/best-embedding-models.description: Voyage 4, Gemini Embedding 2, OpenAI text-embedding-3, Codestral Embed, Qwen3-Embedding, Microsoft Harrier, Jina v5, BGE-M3, Arctic Embed, EmbeddingGemma, Nomic Embed v2 and multilingual-e5 compared on dimensions, context length, price per 1M tokens and license. Prices re-checked on vendor pages in

faqs.question: What is the best embedding model in 2026?
faqs.answer: There is no single winner. On vendor-reported numbers, Microsoft's Harrier-oss-v1-27b claims the top multilingual MTEB v2 score in our list (74.3), and Voyage says voyage-4-large has the best RTEB retrieval results among the API models it tested. The right choice depends on language, budget and hosting. Test two or three on your own queries.

faqs.question: What are the best text embedding models for RAG?
faqs.answer: Through an API, start with voyage-4-large or Gemini Embedding 2, and use OpenAI text-embedding-3-small when cost matters most at $0.02 per 1M tokens. For self-hosted text embedding models, Qwen3-Embedding-8B (Apache 2.0) and Harrier-oss-v1 (MIT) lead the model-card claims, and BGE-M3 is the most downloaded.

faqs.question: What is the best open source embedding model?
faqs.answer: For permissive licenses, Qwen3-Embedding-8B (Apache 2.0) and Microsoft Harrier-oss-v1 (MIT) lead the model-card claims we found. BGE-M3 (MIT) is the most downloaded. Arctic Embed L v2.0 and Nomic Embed Text v2 are Apache 2.0, and multilingual-e5-large-instruct is MIT. Jina v5 has strong scores, but its Hugging Face weights are CC BY-NC 4.0, which restricts commercial use.

faqs.question: What is the cheapest embedding model?
faqs.answer: Among verified API prices, OpenAI text-embedding-3-small and voyage-4-lite are both $0.02 per 1M tokens, and Voyage gives 200M tokens free per account. Self-hosted open models have no per-token fee but cost GPU time.

faqs.question: How many dimensions should I use?
faqs.answer: Start with 1024, or 768 to 1536 if the model supports truncation. Storage grows linearly, and Google's own numbers show little quality loss between 1536 and 768 dimensions for gemini-embedding-001. Confirm on your eval set.

faqs.question: Can I switch embedding models later?
faqs.answer: Yes, but you must re-embed every document and rebuild the vector index, because vectors from different models are not compatible. The exception is Voyage's 4 series, which Voyage says shares one embedding space across its models.

faqs.question: Does a higher MTEB score mean better RAG results?
faqs.answer: Not reliably. MTEB averages many task types and several variants exist, so scores from different sources are not directly comparable. Retrieval-specific scores and your own 200-query eval are better predictors.

faqs.question: What is the best embedding model for code search?
faqs.answer: Test a code-tuned model first. Voyage sells voyage-code-4 at $0.12 per 1M tokens and Mistral sells Codestral Embed at $0.15. Qwen3-Embedding lists code retrieval among its tasks, and EmbeddingGemma publishes an MTEB Code v1 score of 68.76. Compare two of them on real queries from your own repository.

faqs.question: Which embedding models are free for commercial use?
faqs.answer: Check the license, not the download page. Qwen3-Embedding, Snowflake Arctic Embed and Nomic Embed Text v2 are Apache 2.0. Harrier, BGE-M3 and multilingual-e5-large-instruct are MIT. EmbeddingGemma-300m uses Google's separate Gemma terms (EmbeddingGemma 2 moved to Apache 2.0), and Jina v5 weights are CC BY-NC 4.0, which rules out commercial use without a paid route.

faqs.question: Why do some embedding models need a query prefix?
faqs.answer: Many open models learned to tell queries and documents apart through a text prefix. Nomic Embed Text v2 expects search_query and search_document prefixes, Arctic Embed wants a "query: " prefix on queries only, and multilingual-e5 wants a one-line task instruction. Skip the prefix and retrieval quality drops, per their model cards.

faqs.question: What is the smallest embedding model worth self-hosting?
faqs.answer:
In this list, EmbeddingGemma has 300M parameters, Harrier has a 270M version, Nomic Embed Text v2 uses 305M active parameters and Arctic Embed L v2.0 has 303M non-embedding parameters. Small models cut GPU cost, but EmbeddingGemma stops at 2K tokens, Nomic at 512 and Arctic at 8,192. Match that limit to your chunk size first.

/blog/best-headless-cms-platforms.title: 6 Best Headless CMS Platforms for Developer Teams (2026)
/blog/best-headless-cms-platforms.description: The best headless CMS platforms in 2026: Sanity, Contentful, Strapi, Storyblok, Hygraph and Directus compared on verified G2 reviews, published pricing, and what each one is actually built for.

faqs.question: What is a headless CMS?
faqs.answer: A headless CMS manages content through an API without dictating how or where that content is displayed, unlike a traditional CMS (like WordPress) that couples content management to a specific front-end templating system. A developer builds the actual website or app separately and pulls content from the CMS's API.

faqs.question: How much does a headless CMS cost?
faqs.answer: Every platform on this list offers a free tier for small projects or evaluation. Paid tiers for real production use typically start between $45 and $199/month (Strapi, Storyblok, Hygraph), with Contentful's Lite tier at $300/month (€300 in euro regions) and Directus's Team tier at $499/month billed annually. Self-hosted open-source options (Strapi, Directus) can run at zero software cost if you're willing to manage your own infrastructure.

faqs.question: Should I choose a self-hosted or SaaS headless CMS?
faqs.answer: A self-hosted option (Strapi, Directus's free Core tier) gives you full control over data and infrastructure at the cost of managing hosting, upgrades, and uptime yourself. A SaaS platform (Sanity, Contentful, Storyblok, Hygraph, or Directus with its $99/month cloud hosting add-on) handles infrastructure for you at a recurring cost that typically scales with seats, API calls, or traffic.

faqs.question: What's the difference between a document-based, component-based, and database-first headless CMS?
faqs.answer: A document-based CMS (Sanity, Contentful) models content as structured records with defined fields and relationships. A component-based CMS (Storyblok) models content as nestable, reusable visual building blocks a non-technical editor can arrange. A database-first tool (Directus) skips defining a new content model entirely and instead exposes an API and admin UI directly over a SQL database you already have or are building.

faqs.question: What are the best headless CMS solutions for developer teams?
faqs.answer: Sanity, Strapi and Directus fit developer teams best. Sanity gives you an editor configured in code, Strapi gives you an open-source CMS you host yourself, and Directus puts an API and admin UI on a SQL database you already run. Pick Storyblok instead if marketers need to rearrange pages visually.

faqs.question: Which headless CMS has the strongest API for custom development?
faqs.answer: For custom development, Hygraph and Directus give you the most API surface. Hygraph is GraphQL-first and can federate content from other systems into one API; Directus generates REST and GraphQL APIs over a SQL database you already run. Sanity queries content with GROQ and can also deploy a GraphQL API, Contentful has REST delivery and GraphQL content APIs, Storyblok has a REST delivery API plus a read-only GraphQL API, and Strapi ships REST with GraphQL as an official plugin.

faqs.question: What GraphQL support do the leading headless CMS platforms have?
faqs.answer: Hygraph is built on GraphQL. Directus and Contentful offer GraphQL next to REST. Sanity can deploy a GraphQL API alongside its native GROQ queries. Storyblok's GraphQL API is read-only and region-specific, so it is for delivery, not writes. Strapi adds GraphQL with @strapi/plugin-graphql. Check the tier you plan to buy, since rate limits and plan rules differ.

faqs.question: Which headless CMS is best for developers and marketers working together?
faqs.answer: Storyblok, because marketers can rearrange pages in its visual component editor while developers define what each component can hold. Sanity is the other strong pick: several people can edit the same document in real time, but the editor itself is configured in code, so marketers depend on developers for changes to it.

faqs.question: Can one headless CMS serve several websites from the same content library?
faqs.answer: Yes. A headless CMS is not tied to one front end, so several sites and apps can read the same content through the API. What to compare is how each platform separates them: locales per site, roles and permissions per site or brand, preview per front end, and whether references can cross spaces or datasets. On Storyblok, the Growth tiers are limited to one space, so multi-site setups often land on Premium or Elite.

faqs.question: How do you migrate from Contentful or Sanity to another headless CMS?
faqs.answer: Export the content through the vendor's own tooling (contentful space export in the Contentful CLI, sanity dataset export in the Sanity CLI), map each content type to the new platform's model, then import with the target's API and re-point the front end. Rich text is usually the slow part, because each platform stores it differently (Contentful rich text JSON, Sanity Portable Text).

faqs.question: Is Contentful still an independent company?
faqs.answer: No. Salesforce completed its acquisition of Contentful on September 1, 2026. The Free, Lite and Enterprise plans were still listed on Contentful's pricing page when we checked on October 21, 2026.

faqs.question: Can a headless CMS handle multi-language content?
faqs.answer: Most platforms on this list support localization natively, though the depth varies: Contentful and Sanity support multiple locales even on lower tiers, Storyblok scales locale count with plan tier, and Hygraph's entry-level tier caps locale-dependent features more tightly. Confirm the specific locale limits on your target tier before assuming a platform's marketing page claim applies at your price point.

faqs.question: Do I need a developer to set up a headless CMS?
faqs.answer: Generally yes, at least for initial setup. Every platform on this list requires a developer to define the content model (or, for Directus, to already have a database) and to build the frontend that consumes the API. Ongoing content editing after setup can be handled by non-technical staff on all six platforms, though Storyblok's visual editor goes furthest in letting a non-developer restructure a page's layout, not just fill in fields.

faqs.answer: Yes. Syntax shares code in the description of its demos video, Fazt's video runs about half an hour, and Greg Isenberg's video covers the input-plus-questions pattern. For the API itself, TypeSafe's documentation is the source of truth.

faqs.question: How popular are Jev videos?
faqs.answer: The top video passed 350,000 views within days of launch, and twelve videos in our search passed 100,000 views, ten of them listed here. Those figures are snapshots from September 20, 2026.

faqs.question: Do these videos show real results?

faqs.question: Are there Jev videos that criticize it?

TypeSafe lists $0.042 per million input tokens with free output. Prices and free windows change, so check TypeSafe's page before you build.

faqs.question: What are the best LLM tools in 2026?
faqs.answer: The best LLM tools in 2026 are LangChain, LlamaIndex, and the Vercel AI SDK for building apps; Hugging Face, OpenRouter, and LiteLLM for model access; LangSmith, Langfuse, and Weights & Biases for tracing and evaluation; and Simon Willison's llm CLI for testing prompts. Most teams need one tool from the build, access, and observe layers, not all ten.

faqs.question: What counts as an LLM tool?
faqs.answer: An LLM tool is software for building, connecting to, or monitoring applications that use large language models. In this guide that means frameworks, model access layers, observability platforms, and prompt tooling. Software for running models on your own hardware is a separate category, covered in our local LLM tools guide.

faqs.question: What is the difference between LangChain and LlamaIndex?
faqs.answer: LangChain is a general framework for agents, tool-calling, and integrations, while LlamaIndex focuses on connecting a model to your documents and data for retrieval. Many projects use both: LangChain or LangGraph for the application logic and LlamaIndex for retrieval. Note that LlamaIndex the company now puts its main focus on its commercial LlamaParse platform.

faqs.question: Is LangChain free?
faqs.answer: Yes, the LangChain framework is free and MIT-licensed. LangSmith, the company's observability product, has a free Developer plan for one seat with 5K base traces per month, and a Plus plan at $39 per seat per month plus usage.

faqs.question: Does OpenRouter charge more than going direct to a provider?
faqs.answer: No, OpenRouter bills inference at each provider's list price with no markup. Its fees sit elsewhere: 5.5% on credit purchases on the Standard plan (8% on Business), and 5% on bring-your-own-key usage above a free $25,000 of list-price inference per month.

faqs.question: What is the difference between OpenRouter and LiteLLM?
faqs.answer:
OpenRouter is a hosted service you call over its API, while LiteLLM is an open-source gateway you run yourself. Both give you one interface across many providers. Pick OpenRouter to avoid managing infrastructure, and LiteLLM when every request must stay on systems you control.

/blog/best-local-llm-tools-2026.title: 12 Best Local LLM Tools to Run LLMs Locally in 2026
/blog/best-local-llm-tools-2026.description: Local LLM tools moved from hobby curiosity to serious workhorse this year, and the shift caught a lot of teams off guard.

faqs.question: What is the easiest tool to run an LLM locally?
faqs.answer: LM Studio and GPT4All are the easiest. Both are desktop apps with a graphical interface, no terminal required, and a guided model download. LM Studio adds a polished server option, while GPT4All adds built-in document chat. Either gets a non-technical user running a model in minutes.

faqs.question: Which local LLM tool runs without installing anything?
faqs.answer: llamafile and KoboldCpp. Both ship as a single executable. A llamafile bundles the model and the runtime into one file that runs on Linux, macOS, Windows, and the BSDs. KoboldCpp is one binary for Windows, macOS, or Linux that loads any GGUF model you point it at. Neither needs Python or a package manager.

faqs.question: What is the best local LLM tool for chatting with my own documents?
faqs.answer: GPT4All and AnythingLLM. GPT4All's LocalDocs indexes a local folder so you can ask questions over your files on modest hardware. AnythingLLM goes further, with document workspaces, source citations, and agents, and it can run on top of Ollama or LM Studio. Pick GPT4All for the simplest setup and AnythingLLM for more control.

faqs.question: What happened to text-generation-webui?
faqs.answer: It is now called TextGen. The oobabooga GitHub repository moved to oobabooga/textgen, and the project now describes itself as a desktop app for local LLMs. It ships portable builds for Linux, Windows, and macOS, serves an API compatible with OpenAI and Anthropic, and still offers extra backends and LoRA training through the full install.

faqs.question: Do local LLM tools send telemetry?
faqs.answer: Some do, so check before you trust one with private data. TextGen states it has zero telemetry. AnythingLLM sends anonymous usage data through PostHog by default and lets you switch it off in the Privacy settings or with DISABLE_TELEMETRY. For any tool, turn off telemetry and cloud connectors, then watch outbound traffic to confirm.

faqs.question: Do I need a GPU to run local LLMs?
faqs.answer: No, not always. llama.cpp, GPT4All, and Ollama can run smaller quantized models on CPU and on Apple Silicon. A GPU speeds things up and is effectively required for large models or high-throughput serving with vLLM, but you can start on a modern laptop.

faqs.question: Are local LLM tools free?
faqs.answer: Yes. All 12 tools here cost nothing to download and run. Eleven are open source (the comparison table lists each license). LM Studio is the exception: it is closed source but free, and its makers say it is free for use at work too. Your real cost is the hardware and the electricity.

faqs.question: Which local LLM tools support tool calling?
faqs.answer: Ollama supports tool calling (also called function calling) through its API, per Ollama's docs. LM Studio supports tool use through its OpenAI-compatible /v1/chat/completions endpoint. TextGen lists tool calling with MCP support. The model matters as much as the tool: pick one trained for function calling, then test it on your own tools before you rely on it.

faqs.question: Is running LLMs locally actually private?
faqs.answer: Yes, when the tool runs offline. Jan, GPT4All, and a local Ollama setup keep prompts and data on your machine with no cloud round trip. Confirm any remote or telemetry features are off, and avoid optional cloud connectors if privacy is the goal.

faqs.question: Ollama vs LM Studio: which should I pick?
faqs.answer: Choose Ollama if you are a developer who wants a command-line tool and a local API to call from code. Choose LM Studio if you want a graphical app to browse, download, and chat with models by hand. Many people install both and use each for its strength.

faqs.question: What is the best local model to run in 2026?
faqs.answer: GLM-5.2 leads the open-weight rankings in 2026, but its full size needs heavy hardware. For most local setups, pick a smaller open model that fits your memory budget and run it through Ollama, LM Studio, or llama.cpp. Match the model to your hardware first.

faqs.question: Can I replace the OpenAI API with a local setup?
faqs.answer: Yes. LocalAI exposes OpenAI-compatible endpoints, and Ollama and vLLM also serve an OpenAI-style API. Point your existing client at the local endpoint and most code works unchanged. This is the common path for teams cutting API costs or meeting data rules.

faqs.question: What is the difference between vLLM and llama.cpp?
faqs.answer: vLLM is built for high-throughput serving of many concurrent requests on GPUs, which suits production traffic. llama.cpp is a flexible inference engine focused on efficient single-machine runs across CPU, Apple Silicon, and GPU, with deep control over quantization. Use vLLM to serve at scale and llama.cpp to run and tune locally.

faqs.question: Do I need Open WebUI if I already use Ollama?
faqs.answer:
No, but it helps for teams. Ollama runs and serves models on its own. Open WebUI adds a shared, multi-user chat interface with model switching and document upload on top of Ollama or another backend. Add it when more than one person needs a clean front end.

faqs.question: What is a marketing automation agency?
faqs.answer: A marketing automation agency helps businesses design, implement, and manage automated marketing workflows, typically inside a platform like HubSpot or Salesforce: lead scoring, lifecycle-stage automation, email sequencing, and reporting. Some agencies go further and layer AI-driven research, personalization, and reporting automation on top of the platform itself.

faqs.question: Which automation agencies work with marketing agencies?
faqs.answer: ManasFlow is the one firm on this list that automates a marketing agency's own delivery, such as client onboarding and reporting, as custom automation around the tools the agency already uses. The other five implement a marketing platform, mostly HubSpot, for the company that runs it. If you run an agency and want your delivery automated rather than a new platform rolled out, see our marketing automation agency page.

faqs.question: How much does a marketing automation agency cost?
faqs.answer: Costs vary by model. Fixed-subscription HubSpot partners like RevPartners offer predictable monthly pricing. Full-lifecycle and enterprise-custom implementations with agencies like SmartBug Media or Aptitude 8 are typically scoped and quoted per engagement. AI-driven marketing operations automation, our own model at ManasFlow, is scoped after an audit call the same way custom software development is, because the work varies by how many systems and campaigns it touches.

faqs.question: Do I need to migrate to HubSpot to work with a marketing automation agency?
faqs.answer: No, not with every agency. Most of the agencies on this list specialize in one platform, usually HubSpot, and their value depends on you being on or moving to that platform. ManasFlow's model is platform-agnostic: automation is built around whatever CRM or marketing stack you already run.

faqs.question: What is the difference between marketing automation and AI-powered marketing automation?
faqs.answer: Traditional marketing automation triggers pre-built workflows based on rules: a form fill triggers an email sequence, a lead score crosses a threshold and triggers a sales handoff. AI-powered marketing automation adds reasoning on top: agents that research a lead before outreach, personalize content per segment, or generate and QA campaign assets, work that traditionally required a human marketer's judgment.

faqs.question: Which marketing automation agencies have the strongest public review evidence?
faqs.answer: RevPartners has the highest public review volume on this list, a verified 5.0 on the HubSpot Solutions Directory across 450+ reviews. SmartBug Media carries a 4.8/5 across 212 G2 reviews. Aptitude 8 holds a 5.0 across 250 directory reviews. Newer or platform-agnostic entrants, including ManasFlow, have less public review volume simply because HubSpot's directory review system favors HubSpot-specific partners with longer tenure on the platform.

faqs.question: What should I look for when evaluating a marketing automation agency?
faqs.answer:
Focus on four things: (1) whether their specialization matches your actual platform or stack, (2) verifiable public reviews and partner-tier accreditation, not just self-reported case studies, (3) whether pricing is fixed-subscription, project-based, or scoped after an audit, and match that to your budgeting needs, and (4) whether they handle just platform configuration or also the AI and reporting automation layered on top.

/blog/best-mcp-servers-2026.title: Best MCP Servers 2026: 15 Picks Builders Actually Use
/blog/best-mcp-servers-2026.description: The 15 best MCP servers in 2026: GitHub, Filesystem, Playwright, Supabase, and Linear, plus new picks Chrome DevTools, Atlassian Rovo, Figma, and Terraform. What each does and how to pick your stack.

faqs.question: What is the best MCP server to start with?
faqs.answer: Start with Filesystem MCP and GitHub MCP. Together they let an agent read your code, edit files, and manage issues and pull requests, which covers most local development work. Add a database server once the agent needs live data.

faqs.question: Are MCP servers free?
faqs.answer: Many are. Filesystem MCP, GitHub MCP, Playwright MCP, Chrome DevTools MCP, Terraform MCP, and Context7 are free and open source. Hosted vendor servers like Supabase, Cloudflare, Stripe, Notion, and Sentry are free to connect, though you pay for the underlying service. Figma MCP limits Starter and View or Collab seats to 6 tool calls a month.

faqs.question: What is the difference between hosted and self-hosted MCP servers?
faqs.answer: Hosted servers run on the vendor's infrastructure and connect over a URL with OAuth, so setup is fast and the tools stay current. Self-hosted servers run as a local process you launch, keeping data and execution on your own machine. Choose hosted for speed, self-hosted for data control.

faqs.question: Can MCP servers work with Cursor and Claude Code?
faqs.answer: Yes. MCP is a shared standard, so the same server works across Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, Codex, and other MCP-aware clients. You configure the server once per client, usually in a settings file, and the agent can call its tools. For a Claude Code specific stack with install notes per server, see the 12 best Claude Code MCP servers.

faqs.question: Are MCP servers safe to use?
faqs.answer: They are as safe as the access you grant. The main risks are over-broad write permissions and untrusted third-party servers. Stick to official or well-known servers, scope tokens to the minimum, prefer read-only access early, and add approval steps before any destructive action. Our MCP security checklist covers what to check before you connect one.

faqs.question: Which MCP server is best for databases?
faqs.answer: For a Supabase backend, use Supabase MCP, which respects Row Level Security. For deeper Postgres work, Postgres MCP Pro adds index tuning, query plan review, and health checks, making it the stronger pick when performance is the problem rather than basic queries.

faqs.question: Should I use Playwright MCP or Chrome DevTools MCP for browser work?
faqs.answer: Use Playwright MCP when the agent needs to run a flow: navigate, fill forms, click, and check state. Use Chrome DevTools MCP when it needs to diagnose: record a performance trace, read network requests, or pull console errors. Chrome DevTools MCP officially supports only Chrome, so cross-browser testing stays with Playwright.

faqs.question: Is there an MCP server for Jira and Confluence?
faqs.answer: Yes. Atlassian Rovo MCP is Atlassian's official remote server for Jira, Confluence, Jira Service Management, Bitbucket Cloud, Compass, and Loom. It uses OAuth 2.1 and your existing permissions. It only supports Atlassian Cloud, so teams on Server or Data Center need a different route.

faqs.question: Can an MCP server turn Figma designs into code?
faqs.answer: Figma MCP gives the agent what it needs to write the code: a React and Tailwind representation of the selected frame, the file's variables and styles, and a screenshot for reference. The agent still writes and you still review. On Starter plans or View and Collab seats it is capped at 6 tool calls a month.

faqs.question: How many MCP servers should I install?
faqs.answer: Install only what you call regularly. Each server adds tools to the prompt and widens your attack surface, so a focused set of three to five usually beats a long list. Start small, measure which tools the agent actually uses, and prune the rest.

faqs.question: Do I need a custom MCP server?
faqs.answer:
Often the official servers cover the need. Build a custom server when you have an internal system, proprietary data, or a workflow no public server handles. A focused mcp server development approach keeps the tool surface small and the permissions tight. If you would rather have it built for you, our team ships production MCP servers with scoped tools, authentication, logging and tests.

faqs.question: What is the difference between RPA tools and RPA companies?
faqs.answer: RPA tools are the software platforms themselves, such as UiPath, Automation Anywhere, and Power Automate. RPA companies, or RPA agencies, are service providers that build and maintain automation using those tools, or lighter alternatives like n8n, for a client. Buying a tool without the internal capacity to build with it is one of the most common expensive mistakes in this category.

faqs.question: Which RPA tool has the most reviews?
faqs.answer: UiPath has the largest G2 review base on this list, with 7,735 reviews at 4.6/5 for UiPath Agentic Automation as of October 2026. Automation Anywhere is second with 5,718 reviews at 4.5/5, and Microsoft Power Automate is third with 1,093 reviews at 4.4/5. Weigh review volume alongside the star rating.

faqs.question: How much does RPA software cost?
faqs.answer: RPA software ranges from free to custom enterprise contracts. Microsoft Power Automate publishes the clearest prices: Premium at $15/user/month and unattended bots at $150/bot/month, paid yearly. UiPath's Basic plan starts at $25/month and its Community plan is free. Automation Anywhere, Pega, SS&C Blue Prism, Tungsten, and WorkFusion publish no prices, so expect a custom quote after a sales call.

faqs.question: Do I need an RPA tool or an RPA agency?
faqs.answer: You need a tool if you already have internal developers who can build and maintain bots, and an agency if you don't. A tool gives you the most control. An agency or embedded engineer builds and runs the automation for you, at the cost of less direct control over the platform choice. Most teams underestimate how much internal capacity a self-managed RPA rollout requires.

faqs.question: Can RPA tools handle unstructured data?
faqs.answer: Some can, through added document-processing layers rather than the bots themselves. Automation Anywhere ships Document Automation, Tungsten pairs RPA with its TotalAgility document platform, and UiPath includes document processing in its platform. Pure rule-based RPA without one of these layers still needs structured, predictable inputs to run reliably.

faqs.question: Is Microsoft Power Automate a real alternative to UiPath?
faqs.answer: Yes, for teams already standardized on Microsoft 365 and for lighter automations across Office apps. Power Automate wins on published pricing and native integration. UiPath wins on ecosystem breadth, orchestration of bots and agents, and process mining for large, high-volume programs, so the tradeoff is ease of adoption against scale.

faqs.question: What is a software development agency?
faqs.answer: A software development agency is a company that designs, builds, and often maintains custom software for clients, as opposed to a platform or marketplace that hands you self-serve tools or an individual freelancer you manage yourself. Agencies typically own a defined scope of work and are accountable for delivery, not just the individual contributor's hours.

faqs.question: How much does it cost to hire a software development agency?
faqs.answer: Costs vary by delivery model. Dedicated-team agencies on this list start around $25,000-$50,000 minimum project size with hourly rates of $25-99/hr depending on the firm. Project-based full-service engagements are scoped to the work rather than a flat rate. A marketplace like Toptal charges a monthly subscription plus an hourly rate per engineer, typically $60-150+/hr, with no fixed project minimum since you're hiring one person rather than commissioning a project.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a software development agency and a staffing platform?
faqs.answer: An agency owns delivery: it assigns a team, manages the project, and is accountable for the outcome. A staffing platform like Toptal matches you with an individual freelance engineer or a small curated team, but you retain project management, architecture decisions, and quality assurance yourself.

faqs.question: Should I hire a nearshore agency or a local one?
faqs.answer: Nearshore agencies (BairesDev, AgileEngine cover Latin America; Netguru and ELEKS cover Eastern Europe) typically offer lower rates than agencies staffed entirely in the US or Western Europe, while keeping working hours reasonably aligned. The tradeoff is less in-person availability. For most software builds, time zone overlap matters more than physical proximity.

faqs.question: How do I evaluate an agency's reviews?
faqs.answer: Check the review platform directly (Clutch, G2) rather than testimonials on the agency's own site, since those can be selectively curated. Look at review count, not just star rating: a 5.0/5 rating across 3 reviews carries less statistical weight than a 4.8/5 rating across 86 reviews, even though the star number looks lower. Read a few reviews in full for specifics, not just the aggregate score.

faqs.question: What's the fastest way to get a working product built?
faqs.answer: Of the agencies compared here, ManasFlow is the only one that publishes a fixed 30-day delivery window for an MVP as a written commitment rather than a best-effort estimate. Toptal can get you a single engineer working within 5-7 days, but the project timeline from there depends entirely on your own management of that engineer.

faqs.question: Can a software development agency work with my existing tech stack?
faqs.answer: Most agencies on this list, ManasFlow included, specialize in integrating with existing systems rather than requiring a rebuild. The real question to ask any agency is whether they have specific, checkable experience with your exact stack (not just "we know everything"), and whether they can show a past integration with a comparable system.

faqs.question: What is a web scraping tool?
faqs.answer: A web scraping tool extracts structured data from web pages automatically, rather than requiring someone to manually copy and paste information. Tools on this list range from no-code point-and-click platforms (Browse AI, Octoparse) to developer-first APIs (ScrapingBee, Diffbot) to infrastructure platforms built around proxy networks (Bright Data) and marketplace models (Apify).

faqs.question: Is web scraping legal?
faqs.answer: It depends on what's being scraped and how. Publicly accessible data generally carries less legal risk than data behind a login wall, and a target site's own terms of service can restrict scraping even when the data is public. This is a legal question specific to your situation and the sites you plan to target, not something any tool on this list resolves for you; consult counsel for anything beyond casual, low-volume use.

faqs.question: What are the best free web scraping tools?
faqs.answer: Apify, Bright Data, Browse AI, Octoparse and Diffbot all have a free plan, and ScrapingBee has a 1,000-credit free trial. Apify gives $5 of usage a month, Bright Data 5,000 records, Browse AI 50 credits, Octoparse 10 tasks and 50,000 rows, and Diffbot 10,000 credits (vendor pricing pages, October 2026).

faqs.question: What's the difference between a no-code scraping tool and a scraping API?
faqs.answer: A no-code tool (Browse AI, Octoparse) gives you a visual interface to configure extraction without writing code, aimed at non-developers. A scraping API (ScrapingBee, Diffbot) is a service you call from your own code, aimed at developers who want to keep the scraping logic in their own codebase and just need infrastructure (browser rendering, proxies) handled.

faqs.question: How much does a web scraping tool cost?
faqs.answer: Entry-level tools on this list start free or under $20/month for light use (ScrapingBee, Browse AI, Apify's Starter tier). Enterprise-scale extraction, especially against sites with active anti-bot defenses, can run $500-1,000+/month or move to custom Enterprise pricing.

faqs.question: Can a scraping tool handle JavaScript-heavy websites?
faqs.answer: Most tools on this list handle JavaScript rendering (headless Chrome or equivalent) on at least their paid tiers, including ScrapingBee, Bright Data, Apify, and Octoparse. Confirm this specifically for your target sites before committing, since rendering-heavy pages are one of the most common places a scraping tool fails in practice, not in the sales demo.

faqs.question: What happens when a target website changes its layout?
faqs.answer: Every tool on this list can break when a target site changes its markup, since extraction logic is typically built against a specific page structure. The real differentiator is how quickly you find out: Apify and Browse AI both surface run failures and alerts rather than silently returning empty data, which several G2 reviews specifically credit as valuable versus discovering a dead pipeline days later.

/blog/browser-use-ai-agents.title: Browser-Use AI Agents: What They Are and When to Use Them (2026)
/blog/browser-use-ai-agents.description: What makes browser-use agents different from API-based automation, where they are genuinely useful, and the real fragility and security risks worth knowing first.

faqs.question: What is a browser-use AI agent?
faqs.answer: A browser-use AI agent is an AI system that operates a real web browser directly, reading the rendered page and issuing clicks, keystrokes, and navigation commands, so it can complete tasks on websites and applications that don't expose a usable API.

faqs.question: How is a browser-use agent different from API-based automation?
faqs.answer: API-based automation calls a documented, structured endpoint directly, which is faster and more reliable. A browser-use agent interacts with the same rendered interface a human user would see, which is slower and more fragile to UI changes, but works on systems with no API at all.

faqs.question: Are browser-use agents reliable enough for production use?
faqs.answer: They can be, but they're inherently more fragile than API-based automation because they depend on a page's current layout and structure, which can change without notice. They're best suited to systems with no API alternative, or workflows where occasional breakage is an acceptable trade-off.

faqs.question: Is it safe to give a browser-use agent real account credentials?
faqs.answer: Only with the same guardrails you'd apply to any agent with write access to a real system: scoped permissions, approval gates for high-stakes actions, and monitoring, since a browser-use agent logged into a real account can take real, consequential actions on it.

faqs.question: Can browser-use agents be used for automated testing?
faqs.answer: Yes, this is one of the more established use cases. Driving a real browser through a user flow exercises the actual rendered application, catching UI-level issues that a mocked API test wouldn't surface.

faqs.question: Should I use a browser-use agent if an API is available?
faqs.answer:
Generally no. An API-based integration is faster, more reliable, and less prone to breaking from unrelated UI changes. Browser-use agents are best reserved for systems where no usable API exists.

For the safety layer that applies to any agent with real account access, see our guide to AI agent guardrails. For the broader reliability discipline this connects to, read AI hallucination detection approaches. Our AI agent development team builds browser-use automation as a deliberate bridge for systems with no API, with the same guardrail discipline applied to every other agent we ship.

/blog/build-vs-buy-ai-features-2026.title: Build vs buy AI features: what McKinsey's 2026 data means for a 50-person team
/blog/build-vs-buy-ai-features-2026.description: McKinsey's 2026 data shows nearly a third of companies now build AI features in-house instead of buying. For a 50-person team without spare engineering capacity, that stat can be a trap.

faqs.question: Is it cheaper to build an AI feature in-house or buy a tool in 2026?
faqs.answer: It depends on whether you already have spare engineering capacity to own the build long-term. Agentic coding tools have lowered the cost of the initial build, which is why nearly a third of McKinsey's 2026 survey respondents chose to build in-house instead of buying software. But the ongoing cost of owning, updating, and monitoring that build didn't drop, and that's the cost most teams underestimate.

faqs.question: What percentage of companies are building AI features in-house instead of buying software?
faqs.answer: Nearly a third of respondents in McKinsey's State of AI 2026 survey reported skipping a software purchase to build the equivalent functionality in-house with agentic coding tools, according to The Register's August 25, 2026 reporting. Among McKinsey's "high performers," the 6% of respondents attributing 5%+ of EBIT to AI, that figure rises to nearly half, compared with 31% of their peers.

faqs.question: Does McKinsey's build-in-house data apply to smaller companies?
faqs.answer: The strongest build-in-house numbers in McKinsey's 2026 survey come from large enterprises (over $1 billion in revenue, 40% scaling agents in-house) and from "high performer" organizations that already have dedicated AI platform teams. A 50-person company without spare engineering capacity to permanently own a build isn't the population that data describes, so the same conclusion doesn't automatically transfer.

faqs.question: What's the risk of building an AI feature without dedicated ownership?
faqs.answer: The build ships, then loses its owner when the engineer who built it moves to the next roadmap item. Without a maintenance plan, the feature breaks quietly when a model API changes, has no monitoring to catch failures, and becomes harder to fix the longer it sits undocumented.

faqs.question: When should a 50-person company build instead of buy?
faqs.answer: Building makes sense when the feature is core to the product and you're willing to staff a dedicated team to own it past the initial sprint, structured as a proper build engagement rather than a side project for whoever is available. When the need is an internal tool rather than a customer-facing feature, a scoped automation build with handoff included is usually the lower-risk path. For AI agents specifically, our build vs buy AI agents guide covers the five questions that settle most cases, with two cost calculators.

faqs.question: How do I decide between a SaaS MVP build and a custom automation project?
faqs.answer:
If the output is a customer-facing product or feature that needs to scale and get maintained over years, that's a SaaS MVP build. If the output is an internal workflow or tool your own team needs to run, that's a custom automation project, typically smaller in scope with a faster handoff.

/blog/buzz-by-block-agents-explained.title: Buzz by Block Agents: How Identity and Access Work
/blog/buzz-by-block-agents-explained.description: Every agent in Jack Dorsey's Buzz gets its own cryptographic identity and channel-scoped access, not a shared bot token. Here is how agent identity, permissions, and multi-agent handoffs actually work today.

faqs.question: Does every Buzz agent need its own model or harness?
faqs.answer: No. Each agent can be assigned its own harness and model independently, but you are not required to configure one per agent. A workspace sets a default harness and model at setup, and any agent you create afterward either inherits that default or overrides it individually.

faqs.question: Can an agent see channels it has not been added to?
faqs.answer: No. Access follows channel membership. An agent only reads the history of channels it has been explicitly added to, the same way a person only sees the channels they have joined.

faqs.question: What happens to an agent's identity key if you remove it from a workspace?
faqs.answer: Removing an agent from a channel or workspace does not delete its cryptographic key or the audit trail of actions it already took. The signed events it produced remain part of the workspace's permanent record, which is part of what makes the audit log trustworthy: past actions cannot be quietly erased along with the agent.

faqs.question: Is "buzz agents" the same thing as Block's goose framework?
faqs.answer: No, though they are related. Goose is Block's own open-source agent framework, open-sourced at the start of 2025, and it is one of the harnesses Buzz ships support for. An agent inside Buzz can run on goose, Codex, or Claude Code, so goose is one option among several rather than a synonym for how Buzz agents work.

faqs.question: Can an agent modify its own permissions once it is added to a channel?
faqs.answer: Not directly. What an agent can access is determined by which channels it has been added to and what connections have been scoped to it, both of which are actions taken by the person managing the workspace, not something the agent itself controls.

faqs.question: What is the realistic first use case for a team trying Buzz agents?
faqs.answer: Support and internal-ops channels tend to be the safest starting point: contained scope, clear escalation paths, and lower stakes if something goes wrong compared to giving an agent write access to a codebase or a production database on day one. Getting the agent working reliably in a low-risk channel first is also how you build the judgment for what wider access should look like later, which is the core of AI agent development done properly rather than as a one-afternoon demo.

faqs.question: Is Claude Code consulting the same as AI consulting services?
faqs.answer: Claude Code consulting is a specialized form of AI consulting services focused on one toolchain. If you need broader AI strategy or multi-vendor consulting, see our AI strategy consulting page and our generative AI consulting services guide.

faqs.question: What is a Claude Code consultant?
faqs.answer: A Claude Code consultant is a specialist who helps engineering teams adopt Claude Code correctly, covering environment and CLAUDE.md setup, hooks, MCP integration, sub-agents, security, cost control, and team training. The role exists because the gap between installing the tool and running it well across a team is wide, and a consultant brings proven patterns that close it in weeks instead of months.

faqs.question: How much does Claude Code consulting cost?
faqs.answer: Senior, Claude-fluent independent and specialist engineers commonly bill in the $100 to $300 per hour range, while Big Four and large Partner Network firms charge enterprise tier pricing well above that band. Most buyers do better pricing by engagement (audit, setup sprint, embedded engineer, or retainer) than by raw hourly rate, because the unit of value is a working setup, not time.

faqs.question: Is Claude Code consulting worth it, or should I do it myself?
faqs.answer: It is worth it when rollout has stalled, when security or cost questions are blocking adoption, or when you want a proven setup now instead of months of trial and error. Small teams of strong engineers with time to own the rollout can often do it themselves using Anthropic's docs and community resources, and should hire only if they get stuck.

faqs.question: What does a Claude Code consulting engagement include?
faqs.answer: A full engagement includes environment and CLAUDE.md setup, hooks for automated guardrails, MCP server integration, sub-agent and agent workflow design, security and permissioning, cost optimization, and team training and rollout. The deliverable is a working setup your engineers use the next day, not a written report.

faqs.question: Should I hire a specialist agency or a Big Four firm from the Claude Partner Network?
faqs.answer: Hire a Big Four or Partner Network firm when you need global program scale, heavy procurement support, and a single accountable vendor across a large enterprise. Hire a specialist Claude-native agency when you want senior engineers in your codebase, days-not-weeks time to value, and lower cost for the same setup work, which fits most engineering teams.

faqs.question: What is the Claude Partner Network?
faqs.answer: The Claude Partner Network is Anthropic's program, launched in March 2026 with an initial $100 million commitment, to train and support consulting firms that deploy Claude in production. Early partners include Accenture, Deloitte, PwC, KPMG, and Cognizant, and by June 2026 the network had a tiered Services Track (Select, Preferred, Global Premier) and a public partner directory.

faqs.question: How do I vet a Claude Code consultant?
faqs.answer: Vet on shipped artifacts, not certifications: ask to see a real CLAUDE.md, a hooks config, and a working MCP integration from a live engagement. Walk away from deck-first processes, unverifiable badges, no security story, juniors quietly running delivery, or pressure to sign a long contract before a small paid audit has proven fit.

faqs.question: How long does a Claude Code setup take?
faqs.answer:
A focused setup sprint typically delivers a working CLAUDE.md, hooks, MCP integration, security rules, and starter agent workflows in one to three weeks. Driving full adoption across many teams usually needs an additional embedded period of one to six months, because the bottleneck is people and process, not configuration.

/blog/claude-code-for-teams.title: How to Make Claude Code Work for Your Team in 2026
/blog/claude-code-for-teams.description: Set up Claude Code for your team with shared CLAUDE.md files, team skills libraries, CI/CD integration, hooks, and collaboration best practices.

faqs.question: How long does it take to set up Claude Code for a team?
faqs.answer: A basic team setup (CLAUDE.md, a few skills, standardized hooks) takes about half a day. A full setup including CI/CD integration, Agent Teams workflows, and an onboarding program takes one to two weeks. The basic setup delivers immediate value, so start there and iterate.

faqs.question: Does every team member need a Claude Code subscription?
faqs.answer: Yes. Each developer needs their own Claude Pro or Max subscription, or your organization needs an Anthropic API key with sufficient usage limits. For teams of five or more, the Teams plan provides centralized billing and admin controls.

faqs.question: Can we use Claude Code with a monorepo?
faqs.answer: Absolutely. Claude Code handles monorepos well, especially with nested CLAUDE.md files. Place a root-level file with global conventions and subdirectory files with package-specific rules. Claude Code reads the most relevant file based on your working directory.

faqs.question: How do we handle sensitive code and secrets?
faqs.answer: Add clear rules to your CLAUDE.md about files and patterns Claude should never read or modify. Use the permissions deny list in .claude/settings.json to block access to sensitive directories. Never commit .env files, and make sure your skills do not reference real API keys or credentials in their examples.

faqs.question: Does Claude Code work with other AI coding tools?
faqs.answer: Yes. Many teams use Claude Code alongside other tools like GitHub Copilot. Claude Code excels at complex, multi-file tasks and architecture-level work. Copilot is better for inline autocomplete. They complement each other rather than competing.

faqs.question: What if different team members want different Claude Code behaviors?
faqs.answer: Team-level settings go in the committed .claude/settings.json and CLAUDE.md. Individual developers can add personal overrides in their home directory (~/.claude/). The convention is that team settings are mandatory (enforced by hooks and CI) while personal settings handle cosmetic preferences like verbosity and response style.

faqs.question: How do we measure ROI from Claude Code for our team?
faqs.answer: Track three metrics: PR cycle time (from open to merge), number of review rounds per PR, and time-to-first-commit for new team members. Watch PR cycle time closely: in a Harvard study of 718 firms, time from pull request to merge rose 49% after teams adopted AI coding agents, because review became the bottleneck (our breakdown of the study). If cycle time is rising while commits go up, fix review before adding more agents. You can also track the ratio of Claude-assisted PRs that pass CI on the first attempt.

faqs.question: Is Claude Code secure enough for enterprise use?
faqs.answer:
Claude Code runs locally on each developer's machine. Your code is sent to Anthropic's API for processing but is not used for training and is not stored beyond the session. For enterprise security requirements, Anthropic offers SOC 2 compliance, data processing agreements, and the option to use Claude Code through a VPN or air-gapped environment. Check Anthropic's security documentation for the latest certifications.

/blog/claude-code-prompt-audit.title: Claude Code Prompt Audit: We Ran /doctor prompt-audit and /claude-api prompt-audit on Our Own Repo
/blog/claude-code-prompt-audit.description: Claude Code has two prompt audits, and people mix them up. `/claude-api prompt-audit` reviews the prompts and request code inside an app you built on the Claude API. `/doctor prompt-audit` (alias `/checkup prompt-audit`) reviews your Claude Code setup itself: CLAUDE.md…

faqs.question: What does /claude-api prompt-audit do?
faqs.answer: It reviews the prompts, tool descriptions and request-building code in an app that calls the Claude API, looking for patterns written for older Claude models: format instructions that structured outputs make redundant, brittle parsing, removed sampling parameters and thinking settings sized for another model. It returns a findings table and a proposed diff. It shipped in Claude Code 2.1.221 as a subcommand of the bundled claude-api skill.

faqs.question: What does /doctor prompt-audit check?
faqs.answer: It audits your Claude Code configuration: CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.local.md, skills, subagents, slash commands, rules and output styles. On our repo it reported stale paths, references to files that don't exist, contradictions between skills and repeated pressure language. /checkup prompt-audit is the same command. It shipped in Claude Code 2.1.283.

faqs.question: Does prompt-audit change my files?
faqs.answer: It proposes a diff and asks you to confirm each hunk. Its report said Group 2 edits "are proposals for you to confirm," and that none "should be applied as a blanket cleanup." We ran it with editing tools disabled so we could read the report first, which we recommend for a first run.

faqs.question: How much does a Claude Code prompt audit cost?
faqs.answer: It uses your normal Claude Code usage. Our runs on Claude Opus 5.5 cost $4.04 for /doctor prompt-audit on a repo with 17 skills, 2 subagents and a 285-line CLAUDE.md (63 turns), and $1.72 for /claude-api prompt-audit on one 338-line Python file (13 turns). Smaller configs will cost less.

faqs.question: Does prompt-audit work on apps that use OpenRouter or another gateway?
faqs.answer: Yes, with caveats. Our script calls Claude through OpenRouter, and the audit still reviewed the prompts and request code. It marked findings that depend on how the gateway translates requests as lower confidence, because it can't see that translation.

faqs.question: Why didn't prompt-audit read my ~/.claude folder?
faqs.answer: In a headless run (claude -p) the session can't ask for approval to read paths outside the project, so it skips user-level CLAUDE.md, skills and plugins and says so in the report. Run it in an interactive session, or allow those reads, to include them.

faqs.question: Is prompt-audit the same as a security audit?
faqs.answer:
No. It checks whether instructions are current, not whether agents are safe. It doesn't test prompt injection, tool permissions, secret exposure or the skill and MCP supply chain. See what a Claude Code security audit covers.
