faqs.question: What does /claude-api prompt-audit do?
faqs.answer: It reviews the prompts and tool descriptions in an app built on the Claude API and flags patterns written for older Claude models. It is a subcommand of the claude-api skill that ships with Claude Code (added in version 2.1.221). To audit your Claude Code setup itself (CLAUDE.md, skills, agents, commands), use /doctor prompt-audit from version 2.1.283.

faqs.question: Do you offer an AI code security audit as a paid engagement?
faqs.answer: Yes. This guide covers the DIY approach; for a hands-on AI code security audit with a written findings report and hardening work, see our security audit service. For more on the risk landscape, see Claude Code security risks.

faqs.question: Is Claude Code safe for production?
faqs.answer: Claude Code is safe for production when it runs with least privilege, its generated code is reviewed for authorization and injection flaws, and its skills and MCP servers come from sources you have verified. It is not safe by default, because the defaults optimize for capability, not for a hostile environment. Anthropic documents the available controls in the Claude Code docs; an audit confirms yours are actually applied.

faqs.question: What does a Claude Code security audit cost?
faqs.answer: A Claude Code security audit is priced by scope, not by a fixed rate, because a single agent with a few tools is a much smaller job than a platform with many agents, custom skills, and several MCP servers. We give a firm estimate after a short scoping call. That call also tells us how many agents, skills, and MCP servers are in play, which is what actually drives the timeline and cost.

faqs.question: Can AI-generated code be audited?
faqs.answer: Yes. AI-generated code is audited the same way human code is, plus two extra layers: the agent's permissions and the trustworthiness of the skills and MCP servers it uses. The added challenge is volume and speed, since agents produce large diffs quickly, so an effective audit reviews the patterns the agent repeats, not only a single snapshot of output.

faqs.question: What is an agent-skill supply-chain attack?
faqs.answer: It is an attack where a malicious agent skill or MCP server is published to a marketplace or registry, looks useful, and carries hidden behavior that runs with your agent's privileges once installed. The ClawHub incidents in the OpenClaw ecosystem are the clearest public example. The defense is provenance: never install a skill or MCP server you have not reviewed, from a source you cannot vouch for.

faqs.question: How is this different from a normal penetration test?
faqs.answer: A standard pen test targets your application's network and code surface. A Claude Code security audit adds the agent layer: prompt injection, tool and permission scope, secret exposure through agent logs and transcripts, and the skill and MCP supply chain. Those categories do not exist in a traditional app, so a normal pen test will not find them.

faqs.question: Do you also fix what you find?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you want us to. We can deliver findings for your team to implement, or remediate and re-verify ourselves. Because agents, skills, and permissions are our core work, we usually close the gaps faster than a general security vendor would.

faqs.question: How do I choose a provider for this work?
faqs.answer: Look for a team that works with agents daily, tests prompt injection in practice, and can implement fixes rather than only report them. Ask how they handle skill and MCP provenance specifically, since that is the risk most vendors miss. We compare the field in our guide to the best Claude Code agencies.

faqs.question: What is Claude Code security?
faqs.answer: Claude Code security refers to the practices, configurations, and policies that protect your codebase, credentials, and infrastructure when using Claude Code as an AI coding assistant. Because Claude Code can read files, execute shell commands, and take autonomous actions, securing it requires different controls than a passive AI chat tool.

faqs.question: Is Claude Code safe to use for enterprise development?
faqs.answer: Claude Code is safe with proper configuration. The risks come from default settings that prioritize developer convenience over security isolation. Enterprises deploying Claude Code should implement permissions.deny policies, PreToolUse hooks, SAST scanning, and governance rules for YOLO mode before allowing Claude Code access to production codebases or sensitive environments.

faqs.question: What is prompt injection in Claude Code and how does it work?
faqs.answer: Prompt injection is an attack where malicious instructions are embedded in content Claude reads, such as a file, README, or API response. Because Claude processes text from files alongside your instructions, a carefully crafted file can redirect Claude's behavior. For example, a malicious package README could contain instructions that Claude follows as if they came from you.

faqs.question: How do I stop Claude Code from reading my .env file?
faqs.answer: Add permissions.deny rules to .claude/settings.json, such as "Read(./.env)" and "Read(./.env.*)". Claude Code blocks its file tools from reading anything a Read deny rule matches. Also add rules for *.key, *.pem, id_rsa, and any directory containing credentials.

faqs.question: What is YOLO mode in Claude Code and why is it risky?
faqs.answer: YOLO mode is activated with the --dangerously-skip-permissions flag. It disables all human approval prompts, so Claude executes every tool call, file write, and shell command without waiting for confirmation. It was designed for CI pipelines. The risk is using it in interactive development sessions where a misunderstood instruction can cause immediate, irreversible damage.

faqs.question: Are MCP servers safe to install with Claude Code?
faqs.answer: MCP servers are third-party code that runs in your environment with the same permissions as Claude Code. An MCP server from a trusted, audited source is safe. An unvetted MCP package from npm carries the same risks as any unvetted npm dependency, plus the additional risk that it can manipulate Claude's behavior and intercept tool call data. Always review source code and pin versions before installing an MCP server.

faqs.question: Are Claude Code plugins and skills safe to install?
faqs.answer: Only as safe as their author. Anthropic's docs say a plugin you install can run code with your user privileges, because it can ship hooks and MCP servers, so read what it runs before you install one from a marketplace you don't know (plugin docs). Skills are mostly instructions, but a skill's allowed-tools field can grant it broad tool access, and Claude Code applies that field even in a non-interactive (-p) run in a folder you have never trusted (skills docs). Review the skills checked into any repo before you run Claude Code in it.

faqs.question: Does Claude Code send my code to Anthropic?
faqs.answer: Claude Code sends the content of your conversation context, including file content you ask Claude to read, to Anthropic's API for processing. This is how all API-based AI tools work. Claude Code's file tools and file commands it recognizes, such as cat, will not read files matched by permissions.deny rules, so they are not sent. Commands like grep -r can still read them, so keep secrets out of the repo. Review Anthropic's data usage policy and your organization's data handling requirements before using Claude Code on confidential source code.

faqs.question: How do I audit my Claude Code security configuration?
faqs.answer:
Start with a manual checklist: verify your permissions.deny rules cover all sensitive file patterns, check whether YOLO mode is restricted in your team policy, review which MCP servers are installed and their source, and confirm SAST is running in your CI pipeline. Our Claude Code security audit guide walks through the full checklist in more depth. /blog/claude-code-skills-vs-plugins.description: Claude Code skills and plugins look similar from the outside, but they solve different problems. Skills are prompted procedures the agent loads on demand. Plugins are packaged kits that bundle tools, agents, hooks, and MCP servers. Here is when to use each, when to combine them, and the patterns we

faqs.question: What is the difference between a Claude Code skill and a plugin in one sentence?
faqs.answer: A skill is a single markdown procedure the agent loads on demand; a plugin is a distributable package that can bundle skills, slash commands, subagents, hooks, and MCP servers together.

faqs.question: Can a plugin contain skills?
faqs.answer: Yes, that is one of the main use cases. A plugin can ship one or many skills alongside its commands, hooks, and tools. Installing the plugin makes all its skills available to the agent automatically.

faqs.question: Can a skill call a tool the way a plugin does?
faqs.answer: Skills can instruct the agent to use existing tools (Bash, Read, Edit, MCP tools that are already registered), but skills cannot register new tools or MCP servers. If you need a new tool, you need a plugin.

faqs.question: Do I need a marketplace to publish a plugin?
faqs.answer: No. Plugins can be installed from a git URL or a local path. The marketplace is convenient for discoverability and versioning, but it is not required. Many teams ship private plugins via git only.

faqs.question: Should I start with skills or plugins?
faqs.answer: Start with skills. They have near-zero overhead, write a markdown file, commit it, done. Promote to a plugin once you find yourself copy-pasting the same skills into multiple repos or needing tools, hooks, or subagents that a skill cannot ship.

faqs.question: Can a skill and a plugin describe the same procedure?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is a common refactor path. A procedure starts as a local skill in one repo, gets copied to a second repo, and once it is in three or more repos, it is extracted into a plugin. The skill version is deleted from the repos and replaced by the plugin install.

faqs.question: Do skills and plugins work together at runtime, or do they conflict?
faqs.answer: They work together. The agent treats skills from plugins and skills from .claude/skills/ as one set. If two skills have overlapping descriptions, the more specific one usually wins, but this is rare in practice if descriptions are written carefully.

faqs.question: Are plugins the same as MCP servers?
faqs.answer: No. An MCP server exposes tools over the Model Context Protocol; it is one possible component of a plugin. A plugin can bundle an MCP server plus skills, commands, and hooks. You can also run an MCP server standalone, without any plugin around it.

faqs.question: What does "a skill cannot contain a plugin manifest" mean?
faqs.answer: The folder you uploaded as a skill contains a .claude-plugin/plugin.json file, and that manifest makes it a plugin. Either delete the manifest and upload only the skill folder (the one with SKILL.md), or install the folder as a plugin instead, as the error suggests. In Claude Code itself, a skill folder that keeps a .claude-plugin/plugin.json loads as a plugin named <name>@skills-dir, per Anthropic's skills docs.

/blog/claude-code-vs-n8n.title: Claude Code vs n8n: Which Should Run Your Automation? (2026)
/blog/claude-code-vs-n8n.description: Claude Code writes and debugs code. n8n automates workflows between SaaS tools. Pick Claude Code for engineering work; pick n8n for integration logic.

faqs.question: Can n8n replace Claude Code?
faqs.answer: No, because they operate at different layers. n8n orchestrates existing tools and moves structured data; Claude Code produces custom software. n8n's AI agent nodes can handle bounded reasoning steps inside a workflow, but they cannot ship a feature, refactor a codebase, or build an application. If your bottleneck is missing software, no workflow platform replaces the tool that writes it.

faqs.question: Can I use Claude Code inside n8n?
faqs.answer: Not directly as a node, but the practical pattern works well. You use Claude Code to build a small service or script, deploy it, and call it from n8n through a webhook or HTTP request node. Claude Code also ships as an SDK (documented at docs.claude.com), so the custom logic it builds can run anywhere n8n can reach. This is exactly the hybrid architecture most of our production builds use.

faqs.question: Which is cheaper at scale?
faqs.answer: Neither wins universally; the cost models differ. Claude Code costs per token while building, and the resulting deployed code carries no per-execution automation fees, so high-volume custom logic gets cheap once built. n8n Cloud Pro runs around EUR 60 per month, and self-hosting reduces platform cost to infrastructure alone. At high volume, self-hosted n8n plus deployed custom code is the lean combination, which is one reason the hybrid stack is common.

faqs.question: Do I need a developer to use Claude Code?
faqs.answer: Yes, in practice. Claude Code writes and executes code autonomously, but production use requires someone who can review its output, manage the repository, and own deployments. Without engineering judgment directing it, you accumulate software nobody understands. If you do not have that person, use n8n for what it covers, or have an agency like our AI agent development team own the code side for you.

faqs.question: Is n8n really free if I self-host?
faqs.answer: The platform license cost drops away, but not the total cost. Self-hosted n8n means you pay for a server, updates, backups, and the time of whoever keeps it healthy. For many teams that is still far cheaper than per-task automation pricing elsewhere. Details on self-hosting live in the official docs at docs.n8n.io.

faqs.question: Should a non-technical founder pick n8n or Claude Code?
faqs.answer: Start with n8n for anything it can express, because the skill floor is lower and the workflows stay legible to you. The moment a process needs custom logic, judgment over messy inputs, or a real application, bring in engineering help rather than forcing it into nodes. A custom workflow automation partner can also run the whole stack so you never touch either tool. A dedicated n8n agency can build, host, and maintain the n8n side so your team never has to.

faqs.question: What should I automate first?
faqs.answer:
Start with the process that is high-volume, rule-based, and currently done by hand, because it pays back fastest and its requirements are already well understood. Lead routing, data entry between tools, and report generation are typical first wins. Save the ambitious agentic projects for after the plumbing works.

Sources: n8n documentation, Claude Code documentation

/blog/claude-fable-5-1-pricing-benchmark.description: Claude Fable 5.1 shipped September 1, 2026, alongside Claude Mythos 5.1. Base token pricing did not move, but a 75% cut to cache-read pricing and higher scores across every published benchmark are the real story.

faqs.question: What is Claude Fable 5.1?
faqs.answer: Claude Fable 5.1 is Anthropic's first update to Claude Fable 5, released September 1, 2026. It's the same underlying model as its restricted-access sibling, Claude Mythos 5.1, but with standard safety filters instead of Mythos's reduced safeguards for vetted cybersecurity and life-sciences organizations.

faqs.question: How much does Claude Fable 5.1 cost?
faqs.answer: Input tokens are $10 per million and output tokens are $50 per million, unchanged from Fable 5. The actual price change is in caching: cache reads dropped 75%, from $1.00 to $0.25 per million tokens, plus new cache-write rates of $12.50/MTok (5-minute) and $20/MTok (1-hour). Batch API stays at 50% off base rates.

faqs.question: Is Claude Fable 5.1 cheaper than Fable 5?
faqs.answer: Only for workloads that use prompt caching. Anthropic estimates roughly 25% cheaper for typical workloads and up to roughly 45% cheaper for highly agentic workloads, both driven entirely by the cache-read discount. A workload with little or no caching sees close to no savings.

faqs.question: What's the difference between Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1?
faqs.answer: They're the same underlying model with different safety filtering. Fable 5.1 is generally available with standard safeguards. Mythos 5.1 is restricted to vetted cybersecurity organizations (via the Cyber Verification Program) and life-sciences organizations (via the Life Sciences Verification Program), a partnership with the US government.

faqs.question: Should I use Claude Fable 5.1 or Claude Opus 5?
faqs.answer: Anthropic recommends starting with Opus 5 for most workloads, and moving to Fable 5.1 for demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic work, or when Opus 5 at higher effort still falls short of your evals. Fable 5.1 beats Opus 5 on every benchmark Anthropic published except Terminal-Bench 4.0, where Mythos 5.1, not Fable 5.1, posts the top score.

faqs.question: What is Claude Fable 5.1's context window?
faqs.answer: 1,048,576 tokens (1M), with a maximum output of 128,000 tokens. The API identifier is claude-fable-5-1, the reliable knowledge cutoff is June 2026, and Anthropic has committed not to retire the model before September 1, 2027.

faqs.question: Where is Claude Fable 5.1 available?
faqs.answer:
Claude Code, the Claude Platform (Enterprise tier), the Anthropic API, AWS Bedrock, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Foundry.

Sources: Anthropic, Claude Fable and Mythos 5.1 announcement, Anthropic model overview docs, 9to5Mac, Zac Hall

faqs.question: Is Claude Fable 5.1 better than Opus 5?
faqs.answer: On all 9 benchmarks Anthropic published at launch, yes: Fable 5.1 scores higher than Opus 5 on Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, AutomationBench, Humanity's Last Exam (no tools and with tools), Terminal-Bench 4.0, CursorBench 3.2.0, OSWorld 2.0 (partial and strict), and GDPval-AA v2. Most of those leads are a few points. Fable 5.1 also costs exactly twice as much per token. Anthropic's documentation recommended Opus 5 as the default at launch and now recommends Opus 5.5.

faqs.question: How much more does Fable 5.1 cost than Opus 5?
faqs.answer: Exactly double, on both sides of the ledger. Fable 5.1 is $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens. Opus 5 is $5 per million input tokens and $25 per million output tokens.

faqs.question: Should I use Fable 5.1 or Opus 5?
faqs.answer: Between those two, start with Opus 5 and move to Fable 5.1 for demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic work, or when your evals on Opus 5 at higher effort still fall short. That was Anthropic's guidance at launch. Today Anthropic recommends starting with Opus 5.5 instead, which is cheaper than Opus 5 at $4/$20 per million tokens.

faqs.question: Is Opus 5.5 better than Fable 5.1?
faqs.answer: Anthropic still positions Fable 5.1 above Opus 5.5: it is the model for "demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic work," while Opus 5.5 is the recommended starting point for most workloads. Opus 5.5 costs $4/$20 per million tokens against Fable 5.1's $10/$50 and runs with lower latency. Test Opus 5.5 at higher effort on your own evals before paying for Fable 5.1.

faqs.question: Should I use Opus 5 or Opus 5.5 now?
faqs.answer: For new work, Opus 5.5. It is cheaper per token ($4/$20 against $5/$25) and is the model Anthropic's docs now recommend first. Check its breaking changes before you switch an existing integration: forced tool use returns an error and thinking can't be disabled.

faqs.question: What's the biggest performance gap between the two models?
faqs.answer: Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, where Fable 5.1 scores 52.6% against Opus 5's 29.0%, a 23.6-point gap. The next-largest is AutomationBench at 4.5 points. Every other benchmark in Anthropic's comparison table shows a gap of 4.3 points or less.

faqs.question: What is Claude Mythos 5.1, and is it the same as Fable 5.1?
faqs.answer: Same underlying model, different safety filtering. Fable 5.1 is generally available with standard safeguards. Mythos 5.1 is restricted to vetted cybersecurity organizations (via the Cyber Verification Program) and life-sciences organizations (via the Life Sciences Verification Program, a partnership with the US government). On Terminal-Bench 4.0, Mythos 5.1 scores higher than Fable 5.1 (60.9% vs 55.8%), but most teams evaluating Fable 5.1 can't get access to Mythos to reproduce that number.

faqs.question: Do Fable 5.1 and Opus 5 have the same context window?
faqs.answer: Yes. Both support a 1,000,000-token (1M) context window and a 128,000-token maximum output.

faqs.question: Is Claude Fable 5 still suspended?
faqs.answer: No. Fable 5 (and Mythos 5) were suspended from June 12 to July 1, 2026, a 19-day window tied to a US government export-control directive. Anthropic restored both models on July 1, 2026, and they are fully available today.

faqs.question: What is the closest replacement for Claude Fable 5?
faqs.answer: Claude Fable 5.1 (claude-fable-5-1) is the closest replacement: Anthropic released it on September 1, 2026 as Fable 5's successor, at the same $10 / $50 price. If cost matters more, Claude Opus 5.5 (claude-opus-5-5) covers the same reasoning, coding, and agent workloads for $4 / $20. Either way the migration is usually a single model string change followed by re-running your evals.

faqs.question: What is the best Claude model after Fable 5?
faqs.answer: As of October 2026, the current Claude models are Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Haiku 5.5. Fable 5.1 is the most capable. Opus 5.5 is the one Anthropic recommends starting with for most workloads, and it costs 60% less per token than Fable 5.1.

faqs.question: Are all Claude models available right now?
faqs.answer: Yes. Claude Fable 5 and Claude Mythos 5 have been back online since July 1, 2026, after the June 2026 suspension. Fable 5, Opus 5, Opus 4.8, Sonnet 5, and Haiku 4.5 are now listed as legacy models that are still available, behind the current Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Haiku 5.5.

faqs.question: Why were Fable 5 and Mythos 5 suspended?
faqs.answer: They were suspended because a US government export-control directive cited national security concerns. The order pointed to a claimed jailbreak that let Fable 5 find software vulnerabilities in code, and because Anthropic could not filter affected users in real time, it shut both models down for everyone. Anthropic disputed the framing and restored access to both models on July 1, 2026, after a 19-day suspension.

faqs.question: Do I have to switch to a non-Anthropic provider?
faqs.answer: No, you do not have to switch providers. Staying inside the Claude family lets you migrate with a one-line model string change, while moving to another provider requires prompt rework and a new eval set. Add a second provider only if you specifically want fallback resilience.

faqs.question: How long does migrating off Fable 5 take?
faqs.answer: If your model string is centralized in one config value, the core swap takes minutes plus the time to re-run your evals. If claude-fable-5 is hardcoded across many files, expect extra time to consolidate it first. Adding a second-provider fallback is a larger, separate project.

faqs.question: Which model is cheapest if I run high volume?
faqs.answer:
Claude Haiku 5.5 (claude-haiku-5-5) is the cheapest current Claude model: $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens for prompts up to 100,000 tokens ($0.50 / $2.50 above that). It is built for high-throughput tasks like classification, routing, and extraction where cost per call matters more than peak reasoning. Reserve Opus 5.5 for the harder calls and let Haiku handle the volume.

If you are picking a model to power real business workflows rather than just testing it, an AI automation agency can build and operate the stack around whichever model you choose.

/blog/claude-fable-5-mythos-5-government.description: Claude Fable 5 launched on June 9, 2026. By the evening of June 12, it was gone. So was Mythos 5.

faqs.question: Why were Claude Fable 5 and Mythos 5 shut down?
faqs.answer: A US government export-control directive issued on June 12, 2026 ordered Anthropic to suspend both models, citing national security. The government believes it found a method to jailbreak Fable 5 into identifying software vulnerabilities in code. Anthropic disputes that this justifies recalling the models and is complying while it contests the decision.

faqs.question: Are all Claude models down?
faqs.answer: No. Only Claude Fable 5 and Mythos 5 are suspended. Claude Opus 4.8, Sonnet 4.6, and Haiku 4.5 remain fully available and unaffected by the directive. If you need a frontier-class model right now, Opus 4.8 is the closest replacement for Fable 5.

faqs.question: When will Fable 5 come back?
faqs.answer: There is no confirmed timeline. Anthropic has said it disagrees with the directive and is working to restore access, but as of June 12, 2026 it has not stated when or whether the models will return, or in what form. Treat the suspension as indefinite for planning purposes.

faqs.question: What should I use instead of Fable 5?
faqs.answer: Claude Opus 4.8 is the most direct substitute and was Anthropic's flagship before Fable 5 launched. Repoint your API calls from the claude-fable-5 model string to claude-opus-4-8, then re-run your evaluations to confirm quality before relying on it. Our Claude Fable 5 vs Opus 4.8 comparison covers the practical differences.

faqs.question: Does this affect Claude Code or the Claude apps?
faqs.answer: Claude Code and the Claude apps continue to work, because they can run on the unaffected models. Any feature that specifically required Fable 5 or Mythos 5 is temporarily unavailable, but the tools themselves keep functioning on Opus 4.8, Sonnet 4.6, and Haiku 4.5.

faqs.question: What is the difference between Fable 5 and Mythos 5?
faqs.answer: Both share the same underlying model. Fable 5 is the generally available version with additional safety measures for dual-use capabilities. Mythos 5 was offered without those measures to approved organizations only. The June 12 directive suspended both at once. For the full background, see our guide on how to access Claude Fable 5 and Mythos 5.

faqs.question: Could this happen to other AI models?
faqs.answer:
It is now possible in a way it was not before. Anthropic argues that if a "narrow potential jailbreak" is grounds to recall a model, the same standard would apply to every frontier provider and could halt new launches industry-wide. The practical takeaway for builders is to design systems that can switch models and providers quickly, rather than depending on any single model staying available. /blog/claude-fable-5-pricing-explained.description: Claude Fable 5 and Fable 5.1 cost $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens. Fable 5.1 cuts cache reads to $0.25. Here is what real tasks cost, and how Opus 5.5 at $4/$20 compares.

faqs.question: How much does Claude Fable 5 cost per token?
faqs.answer: Claude Fable 5 costs $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens, a 5:1 output-to-input ratio. That's 2x the per-token price of Claude Opus 4.8, roughly 3x Claude Sonnet 4.6, and 2.5x the new Claude Opus 5.5.

faqs.question: Is Fable 5 more expensive than Opus 4.8?
faqs.answer: Yes, on a per-token basis Fable 5 costs 2x Opus 4.8 ($10/$50 vs $5/$25 per million tokens). Per finished task the gap varies: Fable 5 can end up cheaper than Opus on long async runs where Opus needs more iteration, or far more expensive on simple tasks Opus already handles well.

faqs.question: Is Fable 5.1 more expensive than Fable 5?
faqs.answer: No. Fable 5.1 costs the same $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens as Fable 5, with the same cache write and batch prices. The only price change is cheaper cache reads: $0.25 per million tokens on Fable 5.1 versus $1 on Fable 5, so cache-heavy workloads cost less on 5.1.

faqs.question: How does Fable 5.1 pricing compare to Opus 5.5?
faqs.answer: Claude Opus 5.5 costs $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens, so Fable 5.1 is 2.5x more per token on both. Cache reads are close: $0.20 on Opus 5.5 versus $0.25 on Fable 5.1. Anthropic recommends starting with Opus 5.5 and moving to Fable 5.1 for demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic work.

faqs.question: How do I estimate my monthly Fable cost?
faqs.answer: Multiply your monthly input tokens in millions by $10 and your output tokens in millions by $50, then add them. For example, 20 million input and 4 million output tokens costs $200 plus $200, so $400 a month. Cached reads bill at $0.25 per million on Fable 5.1, and the Batch API halves both rates.

faqs.question: How much does a typical Fable 5 task actually cost?
faqs.answer: It depends on the workload, not the sticker price. A quick code review on a 200-line PR runs about $0.10 with Fable 5. Building a full Next.js page end-to-end runs closer to $4. A multi-hour async agent run building a CRUD app can cost around $24. See the workload tables above for the full cost-per-task breakdown against Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 4.8.

faqs.question: Is there a cheaper Fable 5 alternative?
faqs.answer: Within Anthropic's lineup, Claude Opus 5.5 at $4/$20 per million tokens is the obvious step down, and Sonnet 5.5 at $2/$10 is cheaper still for everyday interactive coding and chat. For classification and routing, Haiku 5.5 lists at $0.10/$0.50. For teams that want an open-source option instead of paying per token at all, see our guides to Fable 5 alternatives, the Maestro orchestrator, and Sakana Fugu.

faqs.question: How much does Fable 5 cost per month for a team?
faqs.answer: For a single heavy IDE user, expect around $80/month. For a 4-6 engineer team using Claude Code daily on production work (the "production Claude Code team" profile), budget roughly $1,400/month combined across Sonnet, Opus, and Fable 5 usage. See the full monthly budget model above for lighter usage profiles.

faqs.question: Can I reduce my Fable 5 bill without switching models?
faqs.answer: Yes. Three habits cut spend the most: default to a Sonnet model for everyday work and reserve Fable for tasks that need it, cap max_tokens explicitly on every request instead of letting generations run long, and use prompt caching on long sessions, which cuts the repeated input-token bill by 90% on Fable 5 and 97.5% on Fable 5.1.

/blog/claude-fable-5-system-prompt-leak.title: Inside the Claude Fable 5 System Prompt: 9 Lessons From the 120K-Character Leak
/blog/claude-fable-5-system-prompt-leak.description: On June 10, 2026, jailbreak researcher Pliny the Liberator published what he claims is the full system prompt behind Claude Fable 5 on Claude.

faqs.question: Is the leaked Claude Fable 5 system prompt real?
faqs.answer: It is unverified. Pliny the Liberator has a track record of publishing extractions that later proved substantially accurate, but Anthropic has not confirmed this file, and extraction methods can introduce gaps or hallucinated passages. Anthropic publishes official consumer system prompts in its release notes; the leak goes beyond those by including tool schemas and runtime reminder details.

faqs.question: What is a system prompt?
faqs.answer: A system prompt is the standing instruction set an AI provider places in front of every conversation, invisible to the user. It defines behavior, available tools, safety rules, and output formatting before the user's first message. In the circulating Fable 5 file, that instruction set is roughly 30,000 tokens.

faqs.question: How big is the Claude Fable 5 system prompt?
faqs.answer: The circulating file is 120,040 characters: 17,074 words across 1,585 lines, organized into 72 named sections, including 18 full tool definitions with JSON schemas. That's roughly 30,000 tokens consumed before the user types anything.

faqs.question: Does the system prompt apply to the Claude API or Claude Code?
faqs.answer: No. This prompt describes Claude.ai's consumer chat interface. API requests carry no default system prompt, so you write your own. Claude Code ships separate instructions tailored to agentic coding. That's why model behavior differs noticeably across the three surfaces.

faqs.question: What is "Claudeception"?
faqs.answer: Claudeception is the prompt's internal name for Claude artifacts that call the Claude API from inside the chat interface, meaning AI-powered apps built within Claude itself. The leaked file dedicates a full section to it, including example fetch calls and the instruction never to pass an API key because authentication is handled by the platform.

faqs.question: What's the single most useful takeaway for builders?
faqs.answer: Budget allocation. Over half of Anthropic's prompt specifies capabilities (tools, search, citations) rather than personality. If your agent prompts are mostly persona and vibes, invert the ratio: precise tool-use criteria, worked examples of failure modes, and explicit output contracts.

faqs.question: Should I copy parts of the leaked prompt into my own agents?
faqs.answer:
Copy the patterns, not the text. The structure (named sections, negative examples, worked failure examples, explicit trust boundaries) transfers to any agent system. The content is specific to Claude.ai's product surface and may be inaccurate in places, so treating it as a template rather than a source document is both safer and more useful.

faqs.question: Is Claude Fable 5 better than Opus 4.8?
faqs.answer: On raw capability, yes: Fable 5 scores 91/100 vs Opus 4.8's 63/100 on Every's Senior Engineer benchmark, a 28-point gap. But "better" depends on the task: Fable 5 costs roughly 2x per token (often 3-5x per finished task) and runs far slower, so Opus 4.8 remains the right default for most everyday work.

faqs.question: Is Fable 5 worth the extra cost over Opus 4.8?
faqs.answer: It depends on the task. For quick edits, chat, or well-scoped work, no, Opus 4.8 (or Sonnet 5) is cheaper and just as capable. For large, complex, async-friendly assignments where a wrong result would cost real cleanup time, Fable 5's higher hit rate usually pays for the premium.

faqs.question: Should I use Opus 5 instead of both?
faqs.answer: For most everyday work, yes. Opus 5 launched July 24, 2026 at Opus 4.8's price ($5/$25 per million tokens, half of Fable 5's), and ranks #1 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. It supersedes Opus 4.8 as the default daily driver at the same price point. See the dedicated Opus 5 vs Fable 5 comparison for that head-to-head.

faqs.question: How much slower is Fable 5 than Opus 4.8?
faqs.answer: Meaningfully slower. A typical Opus 4.8 coding response takes 3-15 seconds; the same task on Fable 5 can take 60 seconds to several minutes, and a multi-step async run can take 30 minutes to several hours. This is by design: Fable 5 is built for whole-job delegation, not interactive back-and-forth.

faqs.question: Can I switch existing Opus 4.8 code to Fable 5?
faqs.answer: Yes. Tool use, streaming, prompt caching, and vision all work identically on both models via the Anthropic API, so existing Opus 4.8 integrations port to Fable 5 by changing the model string from claude-opus-4-8 to claude-fable-5.

/blog/claude-md-vs-agents-md.title: CLAUDE.md vs AGENTS.md: What Changed When Claude Code Added AGENTS.md Support (2026)
/blog/claude-md-vs-agents-md.description: Claude Code 2.1.277 reads AGENTS.md when a folder has no CLAUDE.md. Here is the exact precedence, the /config setting, what to do with old symlink and import workarounds, and how to verify it works.

faqs.question: Does Claude Code read AGENTS.md now?
faqs.answer: Yes, from version 2.1.277. It reads AGENTS.md when no CLAUDE.md, .claude/CLAUDE.md or CLAUDE.local.md exists in the working directory or above it. You can change this in /config under Project instructions.

faqs.question: Will Claude read both CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md?
faqs.answer: Not by default. If a CLAUDE.md exists, Claude reads it instead. To load both, set Project instructions to claude-md-and-agents-md. Alternatively, put @AGENTS.md at the top of your CLAUDE.md.

faqs.question: Do I need to delete my CLAUDE.md?
faqs.answer: No. Delete it only if you want Claude to read AGENTS.md directly. A CLAUDE.md that only contains @AGENTS.md is safe to keep and does not cause a double read.

faqs.question: Why does /context not show my AGENTS.md?
faqs.answer: An AGENTS.md that Claude reads directly does not appear under Memory files. It shows there only when a CLAUDE.md imports it. Check the session-start line instead.

faqs.question: Does ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md block AGENTS.md?
faqs.answer: No. Your personal file, the managed organization CLAUDE.md and .claude/rules/ all keep loading alongside AGENTS.md.

faqs.question: Does AGENTS.md work in subdirectories?
faqs.answer: Yes. When Claude opens a file in a subdirectory with the Read tool, it loads that folder's AGENTS.md if the folder has no CLAUDE.md of its own.

faqs.question: Should I use a symlink or an @AGENTS.md import?
faqs.answer: Use the import if anyone on your team uses Windows, or if you want Claude-only notes. A symlink works otherwise, but Edit and Write refuse to write through it.

faqs.question: Does this work on Bedrock or Vertex?
faqs.answer:
Not yet, per the 2.1.277 changelog, and the docs say third-party provider sessions cannot load AGENTS.md. Keep an @AGENTS.md import in a CLAUDE.md for those sessions.

faqs.question: What is Claude Mythos?
faqs.answer: Claude Mythos is Anthropic's most capable AI model as of 2026, internally codenamed "Capybara" during development. It is optimized for complex reasoning, software engineering, and cybersecurity tasks. It is available only as a gated research preview through AWS Bedrock and Google Vertex AI, with no public API access.

faqs.question: Is Claude Mythos publicly available?
faqs.answer: No. Claude Mythos Preview is not publicly available. Anthropic has stated they do not plan to make it generally available and have not provided a timeline for broader access. Access is restricted to approved organizations through Project Glasswing and gated cloud previews on AWS Bedrock and Google Vertex AI.

faqs.question: What is the Capybara codename?
faqs.answer: Capybara was Anthropic's internal development codename for the model now publicly known as Claude Mythos Preview. The codename was revealed unintentionally on March 26, 2026, when a CMS configuration error exposed roughly 3,000 unpublished blog assets including references to the model under that name.

faqs.question: What is Project Glasswing?
faqs.answer: Project Glasswing is Anthropic's initiative to deploy Claude Mythos defensively across critical software infrastructure. It involves a consortium of major technology companies including Amazon, Apple, Google, Microsoft, Cisco, Nvidia, JPMorgan Chase, CrowdStrike, the Linux Foundation, Broadcom, and Palo Alto Networks. The goal is to use Mythos to find and patch vulnerabilities before malicious actors exploit them.

faqs.question: How does Claude Mythos compare to GPT-5?
faqs.answer: On Anthropic's published benchmarks, Claude Mythos Preview outperforms GPT-5.4 on SWE-bench Verified (93.9% vs 81.2%), SWE-bench Pro (77.8% vs 57.7%), GraphWalks long-context (80% vs 21.4%), and USAMO math (97.6% vs 95.2%). These benchmarks are Anthropic's own evaluations and have not been independently verified. GPT-5.4 is publicly available via API; Mythos is not.

faqs.question: How do I get Claude Mythos API access?
faqs.answer: There are three paths: an invitation through Project Glasswing (restricted to defensive cybersecurity organizations), an application through the AWS Bedrock gated research preview, or an application through the Google Vertex AI preview. All paths require a documented defensive cybersecurity use case and Anthropic review. There is no self-serve signup.

faqs.question: Is Claude Mythos dangerous?
faqs.answer: The capability Anthropic describes (autonomous discovery and chaining of zero-day vulnerabilities across major operating systems and browsers) is genuinely dual-use. The same capability that enables defensive security work could assist offensive attacks. Anthropic's decision not to release it publicly is based on this concern. Whether the risk level justifies indefinite non-release, versus a more structured gated rollout, is a live debate among security researchers and AI policy experts.

faqs.question: What zero-day vulnerabilities did Claude Mythos find?
faqs.answer: Anthropic has disclosed several specific examples: a 27-year-old vulnerability in OpenBSD, a 16-year-old flaw in FFmpeg that survived approximately 5 million automated tests, and an autonomous exploit chain built overnight that linked 4 vulnerabilities to escape both a browser renderer sandbox and the underlying OS sandbox. Mythos has reportedly found thousands of zero-days across every major operating system and browser; the full list has not been published.

faqs.question: When will Claude Mythos be released to the public?
faqs.answer: Anthropic has stated they do not plan to make Claude Mythos Preview generally available but that their eventual goal is to enable Mythos-class models at scale with appropriate safeguards. No timeline has been given. General public access in 2026 is unlikely based on the stated roadmap. Watch for developments in independent benchmark verification, regulatory frameworks for dual-use AI, and results published by Glasswing consortium partners.

faqs.question: What is Claude Mythos used for?
faqs.answer:
Currently, Claude Mythos is used primarily for defensive cybersecurity through Project Glasswing: finding and patching vulnerabilities in critical software infrastructure. It is also used by approved research organizations for complex software engineering tasks. Its benchmark performance on SWE-bench (93.9% verified) and long-context reasoning makes it relevant to any high-complexity coding or analysis task, but access is restricted to defensive security contexts.

faqs.question: What is Claude Opus 5's Intelligence Index score?
faqs.answer: Claude Opus 5 scores 51 in max effort mode on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3.2, ranking #11 out of 211 models, as checked September 26, 2026. Claude Fable 5 scores 50, one point behind. Claude Opus 5.5 leads the index at 58.

faqs.question: Is Claude Opus 5 better than Claude Fable 5?
faqs.answer: On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3.2, Opus 5 scores 51 against Fable 5's 50, a narrow win, and Anthropic reports Opus 5 beating Fable 5's best OSWorld 2.0 result at just over a third of the cost. faqs.question: Does Claude Opus 5 beat Mythos 5?
faqs.answer: Not across the board. Anthropic's July 24, 2026 launch post places Opus 5 behind Mythos 5 on cybersecurity tasks: close at finding vulnerabilities on OSS-Fuzz, far behind at developing exploits. The same post says Mythos 5 remains the stronger model for biology research.

faqs.question: What is ARC-AGI 3 and why does Opus 5's score matter?
faqs.answer: ARC-AGI 3 is a reasoning benchmark in which the model has to solve novel problems it cannot have memorized from training data. Anthropic reports Opus 5 scoring three times the next-best model on it, the widest margin in this release, which is a stronger signal of reasoning gains than similar margins on more familiar benchmark formats.

faqs.question: How good is Claude Opus 5 at computer use?
faqs.answer: Anthropic reports Opus 5 surpassing Fable 5's best OSWorld 2.0 result at just over a third of the cost. On Anthropic's Opus 5.5 launch page, Opus 5 scores 74.0% (partial) on OSWorld 2.0 against 81.8% for Opus 5.5. See our Opus 5 pricing guide for the token-price side.

faqs.question: Are Anthropic's Opus 5 benchmark claims independently verified?
faqs.answer: Partially. The Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index score (51 on v4.3.2, #11 of 211) comes from a third-party leaderboard you can check directly. Frontier-Bench, ARC-AGI 3, OSWorld 2.0 and Zapier AutomationBench results are Anthropic's own self-reported figures from its launch materials, not yet reproduced on an independent public leaderboard.

faqs.question: Is Claude Opus 5 good for AI agents and automation?
faqs.answer: Anthropic reports Opus 5's pass rate at around 1.5x the next-best model on Zapier's AutomationBench, which measures end-to-end business tasks, plus a computer-use win on OSWorld 2.0 at lower cost. Both point toward agentic and automation workloads. For new builds, Anthropic's own table shows Opus 5.5 at 40.0% on AutomationBench against Opus 5's 26.9%.

faqs.question: Was Claude Opus 5 the only model Anthropic released recently?
faqs.answer: No. Anthropic introduced Claude Fable 5 and Claude Mythos 5 together, with Fable 5 released June 9, 2026, then Opus 5 on July 24, 2026. Claude Opus 5.5 followed on September 22, 2026, and Anthropic now lists Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 as its current Fable and Opus models.

faqs.question: Is Claude Opus 5 still the top model on the Intelligence Index?
faqs.answer: No. As of September 26, 2026, Claude Opus 5.5 (max effort) leads the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3.2 at 58, and its xhigh and high effort settings hold the next two spots. Claude Opus 5 (max effort) scores 51 and sits at #11 of 211 models on the same index version.

faqs.question: How much better is Claude Opus 5.5 than Opus 5?
faqs.answer: On Anthropic's own launch table, Opus 5.5 beats Opus 5 on all nine listed benchmarks, including Terminal-Bench 4.0 (66.4% vs 52.3%), AutomationBench (40.0% vs 26.9%) and OSWorld 2.0 (81.8% vs 74.0%). It also costs less: $4 input and $20 output per million tokens against Opus 5's $5 and $25. See our Opus 5.5 release breakdown.

faqs.question: Should I still use Claude Opus 5 now that Opus 5.5 is out?
faqs.answer:
Opus 5 is still available as a legacy model, with retirement not sooner than July 24, 2027, so existing integrations keep working. Anthropic recommends migrating to Opus 5.5, which is cheaper per token, but check the breaking changes first: thinking can no longer be disabled, and forced tool use returns an error.

faqs.question: How much does Claude Opus 5 cost?
faqs.answer: Claude Opus 5 costs $5 per million input tokens and $25 per million output tokens. faqs.question: Is Claude Opus 5.5 cheaper than Opus 5?
faqs.answer: Yes. Opus 5.5 costs $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens, 20% less than Opus 5's $5/$25. faqs.question: Should I use Fable 5.1 or Opus 5.5?
faqs.answer: Start with Opus 5.5. faqs.question: What does a typical coding session cost on Opus 5 vs Opus 5.5?
faqs.answer: Using Anthropic's worked example of 50,000 input and 15,000 output tokens, token cost is $0.625 on Opus 5 and $0.50 on Opus 5.5. With 40,000 of those input tokens served from cache, it drops to $0.445 and $0.348. Your real cost depends on how many tokens each model uses to finish the task.

faqs.question: How much do 5 million tokens cost on Claude Opus 5?
faqs.answer: At standard API rates, 5 million input tokens cost $25 on Opus 5 and 5 million output tokens cost $125. On Opus 5.5 the same volumes cost $20 and $100. The Batch API halves every line, so 5 million input tokens on Opus 5 cost $12.50 in a batch job. Real workloads mix the two: 4 million input plus 1 million output tokens is $45 on Opus 5 and $36 on Opus 5.5, before cache reads.

faqs.question: Is Claude Opus 5 cheaper than Claude Fable 5?
faqs.answer: Yes, on a per-token basis Opus 5 is exactly half the price of Fable 5. On a per-task basis for computer-use workloads, Anthropic says Opus 5 beats Fable 5 at roughly one third of the cost on the OSWorld 2.0 benchmark, an even larger practical gap than the token price alone suggests.

faqs.question: Does Claude Opus 5 cost more than Claude Opus 4.8?
faqs.answer: No. Opus 5 and Opus 4.8 are priced identically at $5 per million input tokens and $25 per million output tokens. Anthropic did not raise the price at the top non-Fable tier for this release.

faqs.question: What is the cheapest way to use Claude Opus 5?
faqs.answer: The standard API rate is $5/$25 per million tokens. The Batch API halves that to $2.50/$12.50 for work that can wait, and prompt cache reads cost $0.50 per million tokens instead of $5, per Anthropic's pricing page. If you are not tied to Opus 5, Opus 5.5 at $4/$20 is cheaper on every line. Actual cost per task can still vary significantly based on how many turns or retries a workload needs, which is why Anthropic frames some of its Opus 5 claims in cost-per-task terms rather than token price alone.

faqs.question: Should I switch from Fable 5 to Opus 5 to save money?
faqs.answer: For most general workloads, yes, since on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3.2 Opus 5 scores 51 against Fable 5's 50 (#11 of 211, checked September 26, 2026) at half the token price. If you are moving off Fable 5 today, also test Opus 5.5, which Anthropic now recommends for most workloads at $4/$20. The exception is cybersecurity-specific work, where Anthropic's own disclosure places Opus 5 behind Mythos 5, so that is not a workload to migrate on price alone without testing quality first.

faqs.question: Why did Anthropic price Opus 5 the same as Opus 4.8 instead of higher?
faqs.answer: Anthropic has not published its reasoning for the price point. What is confirmed is that Opus 5 matches Opus 4.8's $5/$25 rate rather than introducing a new, higher tier, while Fable 5 remains priced at $10/$50.

faqs.question: How does Opus 5's price compare across different task types?
faqs.answer:
The $5/$25 rate is flat across task types, but effective cost per task is not. Anthropic's disclosed benchmarks suggest the price advantage compounds on computer-use and automation workloads (OSWorld 2.0, Zapier's AutomationBench), where fewer retries mean fewer total tokens billed, on top of the lower per-token rate.

faqs.question: How much does Sonnet 5.5 cost per million tokens?
faqs.answer: Sonnet 5.5 costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. Cache reads are $0.10, 5-minute cache writes $2.50, 1-hour cache writes $4, and the Batch API halves input and output to $1 and $5. US-only inference adds a 1.1x multiplier.

faqs.question: Why do I get "tool_choice: type tool and any are not supported for this model"?

faqs.question: How do I turn off thinking on Sonnet 5.5?

faqs.question: Is Sonnet 5 being retired?

faqs.question: What is the context window of Sonnet 5.5?

faqs.question: Should I switch from Sonnet 5 to Sonnet 5.5 now?

Switch once your code passes the five breaking changes and your evals hold. However, GPT-5.4 outperforms Claude on harder coding problems (SWE-bench Pro: 57.7% vs ~45.9%). For complex, multi-file software engineering projects, most developers report Claude produces cleaner code and handles architectural decisions better, a gap our [Claude vs ChatGPT for coding](/blog/claude-vs-chatgpt-for-coding) comparison breaks down task by task.

faqs.question: What is Claude Mythos?

It sits above the current Opus tier as an entirely new model class, scoring "dramatically higher" than Claude Opus 4.6 on coding, reasoning, and cybersecurity benchmarks. The "Mythos" name refers to the model as described in the March 2026 leak.

faqs.question: Which AI model is best for business use in 2026?
faqs.answer: It depends on your use case. ChatGPT (GPT-5.4) is best for teams that need broad integrations, image generation, and professional research tools. Claude is best for engineering teams, safety-conscious enterprises, and organizations that need advanced coding and reasoning. Gemini is best for businesses already deep in the Google ecosystem. For custom AI automation that combines multiple models, working with a specialist agency often delivers better results than picking a single platform.

faqs.question: What is the AI skills gap?
faqs.answer: The AI skills gap refers to the growing divide between workers who use AI tools deeply (power users) and those who use them only for simple tasks. Anthropic's March 2026 economic report found that AI can theoretically handle 94% of computer and math tasks, but actual professional use covers only 33%. The gap creates measurable workplace advantages for power users and may amplify existing economic inequalities.

faqs.answer: Both offer consumer subscriptions at $20/month. Claude Max ($200/month) includes unlimited Opus 4.6 with Agent Teams. ChatGPT Pro ($200/month) includes the enhanced GPT-5.4 Pro model. On the API side, GPT-5.4 is significantly cheaper: $2.50/$15 per million tokens (input/output) compared to Claude Opus 4.6 at $5/$25. Claude Sonnet 5 ($2/$10 intro, until Aug 2026) is priced closer to GPT-5.4.

faqs.question: Will AI agents replace jobs in 2026?
faqs.answer: Not yet at scale, but the trend is accelerating. Approximately 72% of Global 2000 companies now operate AI agent systems in production. Anthropic's CEO has predicted AI could eliminate up to half of entry-level white-collar jobs within five years. The most immediate impact is in customer service, finance operations, and marketing automation, where AI agents are already handling tasks that previously required human workers.

faqs.question: Is GPT-5.6 available?

OpenAI has indicated general availability is coming in the following weeks but has not published a firm date. faqs.question: What is the best AI model overall in 2026?

As of March 2026, Claude Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.4 are the two leading models, each with distinct strengths. Fable 5, released June 9, 2026, is now the current frontier model and surpasses both on most benchmarks. The honest answer is that the best AI model is whichever one you invest time in learning deeply. Power users consistently outperform casual users regardless of which platform they choose.

/blog/context-engineering.title: Context Engineering for AI Agents: The Practitioner Guide
/blog/context-engineering.description: Context engineering is the discipline of getting the right information into a language model's limited context window at the right moment.

faqs.question: What is context engineering in simple terms?
faqs.answer: Context engineering is choosing what information a language model sees each time it runs. The model has a limited context window, so you curate the system prompt, retrieved documents, memory, conversation history, and tool definitions to give it the smallest set of high-signal tokens for the task. It is the discipline of managing that window as a scarce resource.

faqs.question: Is context engineering the same as prompt engineering?
faqs.answer: No. Prompt engineering is about phrasing one instruction well and putting knowledge inside that instruction. Context engineering is the broader practice of managing everything the model sees across a whole task, including retrieval, memory, tools, and history. Prompt engineering is one part of context engineering, not a synonym for it.

faqs.question: How is context engineering different from RAG?
faqs.answer: RAG retrieves relevant text chunks and injects them into the prompt. It is one technique. Context engineering contains RAG and adds memory management, compaction, tool scoping, token budgeting, and state that persists across sessions. RAG handles knowledge retrieval; context engineering manages the entire context window.

faqs.question: What is context rot?
faqs.answer: Context rot is the measured decline in LLM output quality as the input gets longer. Attention spreads thin across a long window and the model underweights information in the middle, so accuracy drops even when the right facts are present. Testing across frontier models shows every one degrades as input length grows. The fix is keeping the window small and high-signal.

faqs.question: What is context collapse and how do you prevent it?
faqs.answer: Context collapse happens when an agent repeatedly rewrites its own context, and each rewrite drops detail in favor of brevity until the useful knowledge is gone. You prevent it with incremental, additive updates rather than full rewrites. The Agentic Context Engineering (ACE) approach stores context as itemized bullets and updates them one at a time to preserve detail.

faqs.question: Why does context engineering matter for AI agents specifically?
faqs.answer: Agents run many steps and accumulate context as they work, which exposes them to context rot and collapse more than single-shot prompts. A long-running agent needs deliberate memory, compaction, and tool scoping to stay coherent and accurate. Without context engineering, agents look fine in demos and break on real, long tasks.

faqs.question: What techniques should I start with?
faqs.answer: Start with targeted retrieval, a short-term plus long-term memory split, compaction when the window fills, and tight tool scoping. Add structured note-taking so reasoning survives compaction. Then test the agent at realistic large context sizes, since most failures only appear when the window is full.

faqs.question: Do bigger context windows make context engineering unnecessary?
faqs.answer:
No. Larger windows raise the ceiling but do not remove context rot, since quality still degrades as you fill them. A bigger window without curation often performs worse because there is more room for distractor tokens. Context engineering stays necessary regardless of window size; it just has more space to work with.

For a structured breakdown of every context engineering technique, from context rot prevention to agent memory patterns and window management, see the context engineering mastery breakdown.

Sources: Anthropic: Effective context engineering for AI agents, Chroma: Context Rot research, Agentic Context Engineering (ACE), arXiv 2510.04618, VentureBeat: ACE prevents context collapse, The New Stack: Context Engineering beyond prompt engineering and RAG, Elastic: Context engineering vs prompt engineering.

/blog/contract-review-ai-agent.title: Contract Review AI Agents: What They Catch and What They Miss (2026)
/blog/contract-review-ai-agent.description: What a contract review AI agent actually does against a defined playbook, where a human lawyer still has to be in the loop, and what to check before trusting one.

faqs.question: What is a contract review AI agent?
faqs.answer: A contract review AI agent is an AI system that reads a contract against a defined playbook of acceptable terms and known risk factors, then produces a structured summary of what matches, what deviates, and what's missing, functioning as an automated first-pass review before a lawyer's attention.

faqs.question: Can an AI agent replace a lawyer for contract review?
faqs.answer: No. It automates the consistent, rule-based first pass, checking clauses against a defined playbook and flagging deviations, but ambiguous language, business-context judgment calls, and final negotiation and sign-off still require a qualified lawyer.

faqs.question: How accurate are contract review AI agents?
faqs.answer: Accuracy depends heavily on how well-defined the underlying playbook is and how closely a given contract's language matches patterns the agent was configured to recognize. Testing against contracts with known past issues before relying on it for new agreements is the practical way to validate this.

faqs.question: What contract review tasks are AI agents best suited for?
faqs.answer: Checking documents against a defined playbook, flagging missing standard clauses, and summarizing key terms for a fast read are all well-suited to automation. Interpreting ambiguous or novel language and weighing business context remain better handled by a human lawyer.

faqs.question: Should every contract get the same level of AI review?
faqs.answer: No. Higher-stakes agreements generally warrant a more thorough human review regardless of what an agent's first pass surfaces, while lower-stakes, high-volume, standard-form contracts benefit most from the speed an agent adds to the first-pass triage.

faqs.question: What should I check before deploying a contract review agent?
faqs.answer:
Confirm the playbook reflects your organization's actual standards rather than a generic default, test it against contracts with known past issues, and make sure the escalation path for flagged items, including what requires a lawyer's sign-off, is clearly defined.

For the broader guardrail thinking that applies to any agent whose output carries real consequence, see AI agent guardrails and human-in-the-loop AI automation. faqs.question: What's the difference between custom AI agent development and just using ChatGPT?
faqs.answer:
ChatGPT (or Claude.ai) is a single chat session, useful for one-off tasks. Custom AI agent development builds a system that:

Runs autonomously on incoming tasks (not human-prompted each time)

Integrates with your tools and data

Has measured quality metrics

Handles errors and retries

Operates at production scale (thousands+ runs/day)

The chat product is the tool an engineer uses. The custom agent is the product your end-users interact with (or the internal system that runs without them).

faqs.question: How long does it take to build a custom AI agent?
faqs.answer: For a well-scoped, production-quality custom agent: 8-16 weeks. For a "wow your stakeholders" demo: 2 weeks. Most failures come from confusing the two.

faqs.question: What does it cost to run a custom AI agent in production?
faqs.answer:
Two costs:

Model spend: $0.05-$5 per task at production scale, depending on task complexity, model choice, and prompt caching discipline

Infrastructure: $200-$3,000/month for the surrounding stack (database, observability, eval runner, hosting)

For a customer support agent handling 100K conversations/month at $0.15/conversation, that's $15,000/month all-in. That's still cheaper than 2 full-time support agents for most ICPs.

faqs.question: Should I use LangChain, LangGraph, or the Anthropic Agent SDK?
faqs.answer: In 2026: start with the Anthropic Agent SDK if you're Claude-first. Move to LangGraph only if you need its specific state-machine control. LangChain (the base framework) is fine for prototypes but most production teams move off it for the orchestration layer. Use what's simplest until you've outgrown it. For a full breakdown of all major Python options and their production tradeoffs, see best Python AI agent frameworks.

faqs.question: Can I build a custom AI agent in-house, or do I need an agency?
faqs.answer:
Both work. The question is which is cheaper for YOUR situation.

In-house wins when: you have at least 1 senior engineer with shipping AI experience, you have product capacity, and the agent will be core to your product (worth deep internal expertise)

Agency wins when: you don't have senior AI engineers yet, you want to ship faster than you can hire, or this is a one-off rather than a core capability

The hybrid model (agency builds + transfers to in-house team) is the most common 2026 approach. Pick an agency that designs for knowledge transfer from day 1.

faqs.question: What is the EU AI Act?
faqs.answer: The EU AI Act is a comprehensive regulation governing AI systems in the EU market, structuring obligations around a risk-based tiering system, from prohibited unacceptable-risk applications to no specific obligations for minimal-risk systems.

faqs.question: How do I know if my AI system is classified as high-risk under the EU AI Act?
faqs.answer: The Act lists specific categories considered high-risk, including employment and worker management, access to essential services like credit scoring, education, law enforcement, and migration control. Reviewing your specific use case against these listed categories, ideally with legal counsel, determines classification.

faqs.question: What does compliance require for a high-risk AI system?
faqs.answer: An ongoing risk management system, data governance meeting quality and bias-examination criteria, detailed technical documentation, human oversight capability, and conformity assessment before the system is placed on the market.

faqs.question: What transparency obligations apply to limited-risk AI systems like chatbots?
faqs.answer: Users need to be informed they're interacting with an AI system rather than a human, a specific but comparatively lighter obligation than the full compliance burden required for high-risk systems.

faqs.question: Does the EU AI Act apply to AI systems outside the EU?
faqs.answer: The Act's scope can extend to providers and deployers outside the EU whose AI systems are placed on the EU market or affect people within the EU, which is a jurisdiction question worth confirming with legal counsel for any organization operating internationally.

faqs.question: Is EU AI Act compliance a one-time process?
faqs.answer:
No, particularly for high-risk systems, where the risk management requirement is explicitly ongoing throughout the system's lifecycle, not a single assessment completed before launch and never revisited.

For the ongoing risk-management process this connects to, see our AI risk assessment framework guide. /blog/fine-tuning-vs-rag.title: Fine-Tuning vs RAG: When to Use Each (2026)
/blog/fine-tuning-vs-rag.description: What fine-tuning and RAG each actually change about a model, when one clearly beats the other, and why combining them is often the right answer.

faqs.question: What is the main difference between fine-tuning and RAG?
faqs.answer: Fine-tuning changes a model's underlying weights through additional training, altering its behavior persistently. RAG leaves the model unchanged and instead retrieves relevant information at query time, injecting it into the prompt to supply facts the model wasn't trained on.

faqs.question: Which is better for keeping information current, fine-tuning or RAG?
faqs.answer: RAG. Facts that change over time are a poor fit for fine-tuning, since the model would need retraining every time the underlying information changes. RAG retrieves current information at query time, which naturally stays up to date as source documents are updated.

faqs.question: Can fine-tuning and RAG be used together?
faqs.answer: Yes, and this is a common production pattern. Fine-tuning bakes in consistent behavior, style, or domain-specific reasoning, while RAG supplies current, traceable facts, and combining both often outperforms either approach used alone.

faqs.question: Does RAG reduce AI hallucination?
faqs.answer: It can help, since grounding an answer in retrieved source material gives the model an actual reference to draw from, and the ability to trace an answer back to its source. It's one of several hallucination mitigation strategies, not a complete solution on its own.

faqs.question: Is fine-tuning more expensive than RAG?
faqs.answer: Fine-tuning has an upfront training cost but can be cheaper per-inference since it doesn't require large retrieved context in every prompt. RAG has lower upfront cost but ongoing retrieval infrastructure and larger per-query prompts, so the cheaper option depends on your specific usage pattern and volume.

faqs.question: When should I choose fine-tuning over RAG?
faqs.answer:
Choose fine-tuning when the problem is the model's behavior, style, or task-specific reasoning approach rather than its access to specific facts, since fine-tuning changes how the model behaves consistently rather than what information it has access to at query time.

For the retrieval infrastructure behind RAG, see vector databases for AI agents and RAG as a service. For the hallucination-reduction angle this connects to, read AI hallucination detection approaches. Our AI agent development team scopes fine-tuning and RAG architecture decisions based on whether the actual problem is behavior or knowledge, not a default preference for one approach.

/blog/forward-deployed-ai-engineers.description: A forward deployed engineer builds inside a customer's team instead of from a distance. What the role covers, when it makes sense, and what to charge.

faqs.question: How much does a forward deployed engineer make?
faqs.answer: FDE compensation tracks senior-to-staff AI engineering bands. For a full breakdown by level and region, see our AI engineer cost guide ($300K-460K fully loaded for a US senior hire) and our forward deployed engineer service for embedded engagement pricing.

faqs.question: What is a forward deployed engineer in simple terms?
faqs.answer: A forward deployed engineer is an engineer who works inside a customer's team and builds production software on top of a product. Instead of shipping a tool remotely, they embed, learn the real environment, and build the solution there. Palantir created the model, and frontier AI labs adopted it.

faqs.question: What does a forward deployed engineer do day to day?
faqs.answer: A forward deployed engineer spends most of the week with the customer and the rest writing deployment-specific code, often around a 60/30/10 split between customer-facing work, building, and internal work. The output is shipped software: integrations, custom workflows, and end-to-end systems taken all the way to production.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a forward deployed engineer and a solutions engineer?
faqs.answer: A solutions engineer is pre-sale and helps close the deal through scoping and demos, usually on a quota. A forward deployed engineer picks up after the deal closes and writes production code inside the customer's environment, accountable for the deployed outcome. They sit at different points in the customer journey.

faqs.question: What is a forward deployed AI engineer?
faqs.answer: A forward deployed AI engineer is an FDE whose work is AI: owning the AI strategy and implementation for an account, building agents and integrations, and handling prompting, retrieval, and evaluation. The role exists because a model API alone does not produce an enterprise outcome, so an engineer has to build it inside the customer's team.

faqs.question: Is an embedded AI engineer the same as a contractor?
faqs.answer: No. A contractor fills an engineering seat and executes assigned tickets without owning the customer outcome. An embedded AI engineer figures out what to build, ships it in production, and is accountable for the result, while transferring the skill to your team along the way.

faqs.question: Why are OpenAI and Anthropic hiring forward deployed engineers?
faqs.answer: OpenAI and Anthropic hire forward deployed engineers because model access does not ship enterprise outcomes on its own. Someone has to sit with the customer and build the production system on top of the model. OpenAI started building this team in late 2024 and accelerated through 2025, and Anthropic grew its applied AI group for the same reason.

faqs.question: How fast can I embed an AI engineer in my team?
faqs.answer: Embedding is much faster than a direct hire, which can take months of search and ramp. Through a placement service you can get an AI-native engineer working inside your team in weeks, starting with one defined outcome and iterating from there.

/blog/forward-deployed-engineer-business.title: The Forward Deployed Engineer Business Model, Explained
/blog/forward-deployed-engineer-business.description: How the forward deployed engineer business model actually works commercially: paid for a working deployment, not seats, with the audit-evals-deployment loop that earns trust.

faqs.question: What is the forward deployed engineer business model in one sentence?
faqs.answer: It is a model that pays for a working, production deployment inside a specific customer's environment, rather than for generic product access, so the engineer's incentive is tied to the outcome actually shipping.

faqs.question: How is the FDE business model different from a normal software sale?
faqs.answer: A normal software sale monetizes seats or subscriptions whether or not the customer gets full value. The FDE model monetizes the deployment itself, on the logic that a working deployment drives the usage that generates revenue.

faqs.question: Why do FDE teams stay small on purpose?

faqs.question: Why do FDE salary numbers vary so much between sites?

faqs.question: Is Levels.fyi or Blind data reliable for FDE compensation?
faqs.answer: It is directionally useful, not authoritative. The data is self-reported and unverified, and tends to skew toward people motivated enough to submit a number, which usually means skewed high. Read it as a range with a confidence interval, not a fact.

faqs.question: Does a forward deployed engineer earn more than a regular software engineer?
faqs.answer: Possibly, given the two-judgments premium the role commands (technical judgment plus commercial judgment in the same person is rarer than either alone), but we are not going to assert a specific multiplier without a verified source. Check whether the site names its source. faqs.question: What tools does a forward deployed engineer actually use?
faqs.answer: There is no single required tool. faqs.question: Do forward deployed engineers build custom evals for every client?
faqs.answer: Yes, typically. A golden dataset has to reflect the specific customer's real queries and correct outputs, so it is built fresh for each deployment rather than reused generically across clients.

faqs.question: What happens if a deployment skips the evaluation step?
faqs.answer: The team loses the ability to prove the system works before it fails in front of the customer. Evals are how trust gets earned with evidence instead of asserted, and skipping them is the most common way a promising deployment quietly stalls.

faqs.question: Is observability just logging?
faqs.answer: Logging is the foundation, but observability also means the audit trail is readable by a non-technical stakeholder and that failures can be traced back to a specific step, not just flagged as "something went wrong."

ManasFlow's engineers build agent orchestration, evaluation, guardrails, and observability into the systems they ship through engineer placement, embedded inside your team on your actual stack.

faqs.question: Is a forward deployed engineer just an AI engineer with a different title?
faqs.answer: No. Both can write similar code, but an AI engineer is hired primarily for technical build skill, while a forward deployed engineer is hired for that skill combined with commercial judgment about what to build and for whom, embedded inside a specific customer's environment.

faqs.question: Can an AI engineer become a forward deployed engineer?
faqs.answer: Yes. The technical skill transfers directly. What has to be added is the commercial half: learning to read a customer's real problem, deciding what is worth building first, and staying accountable for whether it actually works once deployed, not just whether it was built well.

faqs.question: Do forward deployed AI engineers write code themselves?
faqs.answer: Yes. Unlike a role that only advises or scopes, an FDE writes and ships production code personally, inside the customer's environment. The commercial judgment decides what to build; the technical skill is what actually ships it.

faqs.question: Why does the distinction matter when hiring?
faqs.answer: Because hiring an AI engineer to do FDE work, or the reverse, sets the wrong expectation. An AI engineer without commercial judgment may build something technically sound that never gets adopted. Knowing which judgment you actually need determines who you should hire.

Through engineer placement: the engineer embeds with your team, brings the technical build skill of an AI engineer, and applies the commercial judgment of an FDE to decide what is actually worth building in your stack.

faqs.question: Is a forward deployed engineer more expensive than a consultant?

faqs.question: Can a consultant become a forward deployed engineer on the same project?

faqs.answer: Hire a consultant when you need an outside opinion, a feasibility study, or a roadmap before you commit engineering time. Hire an FDE when the plan is already clear enough and what you need is someone to build and ship it.

faqs.question: Do forward deployed engineers replace an internal engineering team?

faqs.question: What is a fractional CAIO?
faqs.answer: A fractional CAIO is a part-time chief AI officer who owns your AI strategy, governance, build-versus-buy decisions, and board reporting on a fixed monthly retainer. It is the same role as a full-time CAIO, compressed into a part-time, outcome-focused cadence.

faqs.question: How much does a fractional CAIO cost?
faqs.answer: A fractional CAIO typically costs $5K to $30K per month, or roughly $60K to $180K per year, versus $300K to $550K-plus for a full-time hire (iternal.ai). Senior independent operators can charge more, up to $20K to $80K per month at the top of the market.

faqs.question: What does a fractional CAIO do?
faqs.answer: A fractional CAIO sets AI strategy and roadmap, establishes governance and risk controls, makes build-versus-buy calls, builds internal capability, and reports progress to the board (theaihat). The focus shifts from assessment early on to governance and capability transfer later.

faqs.question: Is a fractional CAIO the same as an AI consultant?
faqs.answer: No. A fractional CAIO is embedded executive leadership accountable for outcomes, while an AI consultant typically delivers a defined project or assessment and then leaves. The CAIO owns results over time, not advice alone.

faqs.question: When should a company hire a fractional CAIO?
faqs.answer: Hire one when AI is strategic but a full-time CAIO is premature, usually below roughly $300M in revenue or at Series A through Series C (iternal.ai). It also fits when you need governance owned or your board is asking about AI and nobody internally owns the answer.

faqs.question: How is a fractional CAIO different from a fractional CTO?
faqs.answer: A fractional CAIO focuses specifically on AI strategy, governance, and board reporting, while a fractional CTO owns broad engineering and technical direction with AI as one part. If AI is the central question, the CAIO fits; if general technical leadership is the gap, the CTO fits. Our fractional CTO versus CAIO guide breaks this down further.

faqs.question: Does a fractional CAIO actually build the AI systems?
faqs.answer: A fractional CAIO owns strategy and direction, then either directs your existing engineers or brings in a delivery team to build. ManasFlow pairs the CAIO role with AI agent development and embedded engineer placement so the roadmap turns into working systems.

faqs.question: What results do companies with a CAIO see?
faqs.answer:
IBM found that organizations with a chief AI officer report around 10% higher return on AI investment, and CAIO adoption grew from 26% to 76% of surveyed firms in a single year (IBM). A dedicated AI owner correlates with measurably better AI outcomes.
