faqs.question: What is a fractional CTO in simple terms?
faqs.answer: A fractional CTO is a part-time senior technology leader who owns your engineering strategy and execution without a full-time salary. You buy a fraction of an executive's time, usually on a monthly retainer, and they stay embedded in your team rather than delivering a one-off report.

faqs.question: How much does a fractional CTO cost in 2026?
faqs.answer: Published 2026 pricing guides put fractional CTO monthly retainers at roughly 5,000 to 15,000 US dollars for a 10 to 20 hour per week engagement, with hourly rates reported between about 150 and 500 US dollars per hour. The exact figure depends on company stage, scope, and the authority you grant, so treat ranges as context rather than a quote.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a fractional CTO and a fractional CAIO?
faqs.answer: A fractional CTO covers technology broadly, including infrastructure, hiring, and delivery, while a fractional CAIO focuses only on AI strategy, governance, and adoption. Companies with a serious AI mandate often run both at once, because deep AI ownership is a different job from general engineering leadership.

faqs.question: When should a startup hire a fractional CTO instead of a full-time one?
faqs.answer: Hire fractional when you need senior technical judgment but cannot yet justify a permanent executive, which is common before Series A and during early scaling. A full-time hire makes sense once the scope is sustained enough to justify a loaded annual cost that can exceed 400,000 US dollars.

faqs.question: Is a fractional CTO the same as an interim CTO?
faqs.answer: No. An interim CTO is a temporary placeholder, often full-time for three to six months, who covers a sudden leadership gap while you hire a permanent executive. A fractional CTO is an ongoing, part-time partner who stays as long as the arrangement serves the business.

faqs.question: Do I need a fractional CTO or a fractional CAIO for AI strategy?
faqs.answer: If AI is your specific bottleneck and no one owns the roadmap, governance, or adoption, a fractional CAIO is the better fit. A fractional CTO can lead early AI work, but their attention is split across all of technology, so a dedicated AI leader moves faster on AI alone.

faqs.question: Can a fractional engagement turn into a full-time role?
faqs.answer:
Yes, and that is a common path. Many companies start fractional, let the leader establish strategy and governance, confirm the value, and then convert to a full-time hire once the scope and requirements are clearly defined.

faqs.question: Can I use free AI models commercially?
faqs.answer: Yes, if the model's license permits commercial use and, for hosted access, the provider's terms allow it on your tier. Open weights under Apache-2.0 or MIT, such as FLUX.1 schnell and Whisper large-v3, are safe defaults. Free API tiers are the riskier category, because many prohibit commercial use regardless of the underlying model's license.

faqs.question: Is DeepSeek free for commercial use?
faqs.answer: DeepSeek's open weights allow commercial use, but under the DeepSeek Model License, which carries its own conditions and is not MIT. The code repositories are permissively licensed, which causes confusion, but the weights are governed by the model license. Read that license text before building a product on DeepSeek weights, and re-verify it periodically since terms can change.

faqs.question: Can I use the ElevenLabs free tier commercially?
faqs.answer: No. The ElevenLabs free tier is non-commercial and requires attribution, so audio generated on it cannot be used in a revenue-generating product or client work. If you need the voices commercially, you need a paid plan whose terms grant a commercial license to the generated audio.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a model license and API terms?
faqs.answer: A model license governs the weights file you download; API terms govern the hosted service you call. Self-hosting an Apache-2.0 model gives you the rights in that license. Calling the same model through a provider's free endpoint binds you to the provider's terms instead, which may be evaluation-only. Always check the document that matches how you actually access the model.

faqs.question: Is FLUX.1 schnell really free for commercial images?
faqs.answer: Yes. FLUX.1 schnell is released under Apache-2.0, which permits commercial use of the model and its outputs without a fee. The catch is the variant: FLUX.1 dev, the higher-quality sibling, uses a non-commercial license. Confirm your pipeline loads the schnell checkpoint specifically, and keep a dated copy of the license text you relied on.

faqs.question: Do free API tiers use my data for training?
faqs.answer: Many do, and the permission is usually buried in the terms of service rather than the pricing page. If you send confidential business data, client material, or personal information through a free endpoint, check the data-use clause first. Paid tiers frequently offer opt-outs that free tiers do not, which is one more reason free tiers rarely survive contact with production. If you are unsure how to structure this, our custom automation team handles data routing and provider selection as part of every build.

faqs.question: How do I keep track of license changes after I ship?
faqs.answer:
Archive a dated copy of every license and terms document you relied on, then re-check them on a schedule, quarterly at minimum. Licenses and free-tier terms change without much announcement. Our /free-models directory tracks 297 models with a commercial-use column and the current catch per model, which makes the periodic re-check faster.

faqs.question: Is generative AI consulting different from regular AI consulting?
faqs.answer:
In 2026, "AI consulting" and "generative AI consulting" have effectively merged. The distinction made sense in 2022-2023 when classical ML and LLM work required different teams. Today, any consultancy doing serious "AI consulting" is mostly doing GenAI/LLM work, with some classical ML in narrow verticals (computer vision, time-series forecasting).

If a partner draws a hard distinction between "traditional AI" and "generative AI," they're either niche specialists (legit) or they're behind the market (not legit).

faqs.question: How long until generative AI consulting pays back?
faqs.answer:
Best case: 60-90 days for a sharply-scoped automation that eliminates clear manual work. Typical case: 4-9 months. Worst case (and most common reason for failure): payback never materializes because the project shipped but no one uses it.

The single biggest predictor of payback: was the use case chosen because it was easy to demo, or because the manual version of the work was actually expensive? The first kind ships and gets ignored; the second pays back fast.

faqs.question: What's the difference between consulting and development services?
faqs.answer:
Consulting = thinking, strategy, evaluation, vendor selection. Output is usually a deck, a roadmap, or a recommendation. Development services = building. Output is shipped product.

The best 2026 partners do both, sequenced sensibly: a short strategy phase that ends with a concrete build target, then most of the engagement spent shipping.

faqs.question: Should I hire one big consultancy or several specialized ones?
faqs.answer:
For most companies (under 5,000 employees), one specialized partner who does both strategy and execution is better than a Big Four firm + a separate dev shop. The handoff between firms is where most projects die.

For enterprise (5,000+ employees, regulated industries), a hybrid approach can work: a large firm for change management and stakeholder alignment, a smaller specialized firm for actual engineering. But the smaller firm has to ship; the large firm can't backstop technical depth.

faqs.question: How do I measure if the engagement is working?
faqs.answer:
Three metrics that matter, ranked by signal quality:

Demoable progress every 2 weeks. If you can't watch something work better in a sandbox after sprint 1, the project is in trouble.

Eval metrics improving over time. Accuracy, latency, cost per task: pick the ones that matter for your use case and watch them weekly.

Knowledge transfer happening continuously. Your team should be able to make small changes to prompts, evals, and tooling by week 4. If they can't, you're building dependency, not capability.

/blog/geo-optimization-for-ai-search.title: AEO and GEO for AI Search: A Practical Guide (2026)
/blog/geo-optimization-for-ai-search.description: What GEO (Generative Engine Optimization) actually changes about content structure, how it differs from traditional SEO, and a practical checklist to make a page citable by ChatGPT and Perplexity.

faqs.question: What is AEO, and is it the same thing as GEO?
faqs.answer: Mostly, yes. AEO (Answer Engine Optimization) and GEO describe the same underlying practice; AEO is often used specifically for question-and-answer content, while GEO is the broader umbrella term covering any AI-generated answer surface.

faqs.question: What is GEO in SEO?
faqs.answer: GEO stands for Generative Engine Optimization: structuring content so AI systems like ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google AI Overviews can retrieve, understand, and cite it as a source, rather than optimizing purely for a ranked list of blue links.

faqs.question: Does GEO replace SEO?
faqs.answer: No. GEO is additive. A page still needs to rank well and load fast, but it also needs answer-first structure, clean schema markup, and specific, checkable claims to get pulled into an AI-generated answer once it's found.

faqs.question: How long does it take to see GEO results?
faqs.answer: There's no fixed timeline, because AI citation tracking is still immature and crawl/retrieval cycles vary by engine. Most teams treat it as a 60-to-90-day structural change (rewriting key pages for answer-first structure and schema) followed by ongoing manual testing against real prompts.

faqs.question: Do I need new content, or can I optimize what I already have?
faqs.answer: Existing high-value pages are usually the better starting point. Audit pages that already rank for commercial or informational queries, restructure the top of each key section to lead with a direct answer, add FAQ schema, and turn any comparative claims into tables before writing anything new.

faqs.question: What tools track AI citations?
faqs.answer: The space is early and fragmented. Manual prompt testing against ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini remains the most reliable method today, supplemented by watching referral traffic from AI chat interfaces in your analytics and tracking branded search lift in Search Console.

faqs.question: Does schema markup actually help GEO?
faqs.answer:
Yes, directionally. FAQPage, Article, and Organization JSON-LD give retrieval systems unambiguous structure to parse instead of forcing them to infer intent from raw HTML, which reduces the chance of a model skipping or misreading your content.

/blog/graphrag.description: GraphRAG retrieves from a knowledge graph instead of just ranking text chunks by similarity, which makes it better at multi-hop and relationship questions and worse at cost and maintenance. Here's what it actually is, how the extraction-to-traversal pipeline works, and when the graph is worth the ov

faqs.question: What is GraphRAG in simple terms?
faqs.answer: GraphRAG is retrieval-augmented generation that retrieves from a knowledge graph, entities and their relationships, instead of only ranking text chunks by similarity. It answers questions that depend on how facts connect, not just which text sounds similar to the query.

faqs.question: How is GraphRAG different from a knowledge graph?
faqs.answer: A knowledge graph is a data structure: nodes for entities, edges for relationships. GraphRAG is the retrieval architecture that builds a knowledge graph from your documents and queries it at inference time to feed an LLM. The graph is the data; GraphRAG is what you do with it at query time.

faqs.question: Does GraphRAG replace vector RAG?
faqs.answer: No. Most production systems run both, using the vector index for chunk-level similarity search and the graph for relationship and multi-hop queries, then combine the results. Pure graph-only retrieval is uncommon outside research settings.

faqs.question: Is GraphRAG more expensive than vector RAG?
faqs.answer: Yes, on both ingestion and maintenance. Entity and relationship extraction runs an LLM pass over your corpus that vector RAG doesn't need, and keeping entity resolution accurate as new documents arrive is ongoing work. Query-time traversal is also typically slower than a single vector similarity search.

faqs.question: What tools support GraphRAG?
faqs.answer: Neo4j has native GraphRAG tooling, LlamaIndex ships a PropertyGraphIndex, and LangChain has graph-retrieval modules. Microsoft's original GraphRAG implementation, released as open source in 2024, is also a common starting point for the community-summarization pattern.

faqs.question: When should I not use GraphRAG?
faqs.answer: When your actual queries are single-fact lookups or general semantic search, and your corpus doesn't have a stable, meaningful entity model. In that case a vector index alone is faster to build, cheaper to run, and answers the same questions just as well.

faqs.question: How long does a GraphRAG build take?
faqs.answer:
Longer than a vector RAG build of the same corpus, mainly because entity resolution needs tuning against real documents, not a fixed timeline. A working prototype can come together in a few weeks; getting entity resolution accurate enough for production use is usually the phase that takes longer than teams expect.

Sources: Microsoft Research, "From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization", Microsoft GraphRAG open-source project, Neo4j, "What Is GraphRAG?", LlamaIndex PropertyGraphIndex documentation

faqs.question: What is Grok Bot?
faqs.answer: Grok Bot is xAI's always-on AI agent product, launched in beta on August 11, 2026. faqs.question: Is Grok Bot free?
faqs.answer: Not as an ongoing plan. Cursor's help page describes a free trial given as a usage credit, measured by agent steps and tokens, with a 7-day window. After that you need Premium, Super or Ultra on The X Subscription, a legacy Cursor plan (Pro, Pro+, Ultra or Teams), or a linked SuperGrok or X Premium+ account. faqs.question: Which plans include Grok Bot?
faqs.answer: As of October 23, 2026, Cursor's help page lists Premium, Super and Ultra on The X Subscription (individual and team seats), legacy Cursor Pro, Pro+, Ultra and Teams, linked SuperGrok, SuperGrok Plus, SuperGrok Heavy or X Premium+ accounts, and seats on a self-serve Grok Business plan. Free and Plus on The X Subscription do not include it. SuperGrok Lite, SuperGrok Team and SuperGrok Enterprise cannot link. Cursor Enterprise access goes through your account executive.

faqs.question: How much does Grok Bot cost?
faqs.answer: Grok Bot has no separate subscription. On Cursor's pricing page (October 23, 2026), it is included from the Premium tier of The X Subscription at $30 a month, then Super at $100 and Ultra at $200, with Teams from $30 per user. Plus ($8) and Free do not include it. Legacy Cursor Pro, Pro+ and Ultra plans still include it. Extra usage past the weekly pool is paid from prepaid credit.

faqs.question: Is Grok Bot the same as @grok on X?
faqs.answer: No. Grok Bot is xAI's agent product with its own apps and cloud computer. The @grok account on X is a different way to reach Grok. xAI's Grok Bot pages do not cover @grok, so check X's own help pages for how it works.

faqs.question: How do I set up Grok Bot?
faqs.answer: Per xAI's docs, create a Bot, describe its job in a message, then grant it access to the tools it needs. Install the desktop app or the mobile app and sign in with your Cursor account. Some websites block automation or ask you to step in.

faqs.question: What devices does Grok Bot run on?
faqs.answer: xAI's docs list desktop apps for macOS, Windows and Linux, and mobile apps for iPhone, iPad and Android. Everything runs on a cloud computer, so work continues when your device is off. Docs checked September 26, 2026 at docs.x.ai/grok-bot/overview.

faqs.question: How is Grok Bot different from Grok chat?
faqs.answer: Grok chat answers you inside a conversation. Grok Bot runs agents on a cloud computer that sign into your apps, do multi-step work in the real tools, and keep going when you close the app. On The X Subscription, Grok Bot draws from the same weekly pool as Cursor and the Grok apps, so long Bot jobs do eat into your chat and coding usage. On legacy Cursor plans and linked accounts, Grok Bot has its own weekly allowance.

faqs.question: Is Grok Bot available on Android?
faqs.answer: Yes. As of September 26, 2026, Cursor's Grok Bot mobile help page says the app is available on iOS and Android, installed from the App Store or Google Play. You sign in with the same Cursor account and get the same cloud computer as on desktop. The desktop app runs on macOS, Windows and Linux.

faqs.question: How is Grok Bot different from a regular AI chatbot?
faqs.answer: A regular AI chatbot produces its output inside the chat window and stops working when you close it. Grok Bot's agents run on a cloud computer, keep working when your device is off, and produce output directly inside the tool being used (an inbox, a CRM, a document) rather than in the chat.

faqs.question: Can I choose which AI model Grok Bot uses for a task?
faqs.answer: No. Cursor's Grok Bot settings docs say Cursor manages model selection and there is no model picker. This is a limitation for technical teams with specific model requirements.

faqs.question: What is the "teach a task" feature in Grok Bot?
faqs.answer: Teach a task puts a Bot into a recording mode where you demonstrate a browser workflow step by step. The Bot turns the recording into a draft skill it can repeat, including on a schedule through routines. Cursor's docs say the feature is rolling out gradually, so it may not appear on every account yet.

faqs.question: Should a business build a custom AI agent instead of using Grok Bot?
faqs.answer:
It depends on the workflow. Off-the-shelf tools like Grok Bot are built for breadth across common tasks. A workflow with specific compliance, model, or internal-tool requirements that Grok Bot cannot meet is a better fit for custom AI agent development.

faqs.answer: GEO is the practice of structuring content so AI answer engines cite it as a source in their generated responses. It targets citations inside answers from ChatGPT, Perplexity, and similar engines, rather than ranked links in a traditional results page.

faqs.question: How do I get cited by ChatGPT and Perplexity?
faqs.answer: Lead with answer-first blocks of 40 to 60 words, add FAQPage schema, include attributed statistics, cite credible sources in your copy, earn brand mentions across the web, and keep pages fresh. Princeton-led research found citations, quotations, and statistics lift AI source visibility by 30 to 40% (SEO.ai).

faqs.question: Is GEO different from SEO?
faqs.answer: Yes. SEO optimizes for ranked links and clicks; GEO optimizes for citations inside AI answers. They share crawlability and authority foundations, so strong technical SEO supports GEO, but the success metrics differ.

faqs.question: Does llms.txt actually work?
faqs.answer: Not reliably yet. llms.txt is a proposed convention with no standards-body backing, and no major AI provider has confirmed reading it in production as of early 2026 (Bluehost). Publishing it is low-cost and forward-looking, but it is not a dependable ranking lever today.

faqs.question: Which content format gets cited most?
faqs.answer: Content with clear headings, bullets, tables, and self-contained answer blocks. Such structured content is reported as 28 to 40% more likely to be cited because models can extract a clean, unambiguous passage (SEO.ai).

faqs.question: How long does GEO take to show results?
faqs.answer: Many brands report measurable changes in AI citation frequency within roughly 4 to 8 weeks of deploying schema, answer-first structure, and citable statistics (Frase). Entity and brand-mention work compounds more slowly over months.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a mention and a citation?
faqs.answer: A mention is your brand appearing in an AI answer. A citation is the engine naming your page as the source for a claim. Citations carry more authority weight and are the stronger GEO outcome (Averi).

faqs.question: How do I measure whether GEO is working?
faqs.answer:
Track citation frequency, share of voice against competitors, source domain coverage, and conversion from AI-referred traffic. Use monitoring tools like Profound or Semrush, or run a manual monthly audit of 20 buyer questions across each engine (digitalapplied).

For teams choosing which Claude model to use in the AI-native search stack they are optimizing for, the Fable 5 vs Opus 4.8 comparison covers capability and cost tradeoffs.

faqs.question: How do I hire a forward deployed engineer?
faqs.answer: Screen for both technical and commercial judgment separately, ask for a real audit and a real eval set (not just a portfolio of finished demos), and confirm who is accountable for the production outcome. If you would rather not run that search yourself, an embedded placement partner like ManasFlow's engineer placement can match you with an engineer who already works this way.

faqs.question: What does a forward deployed engineer cost?
faqs.answer: There is no verified, universal number. Varick Agents' guide states a range of $150K to $1M depending on scope and seniority; treat that as their estimate, not a fact. If you engage through a placement model, ask for a published number and timeline rather than a quote that only appears after a sales call.

faqs.question: What questions should I ask when hiring an FDE?
faqs.answer: Ask them to describe a real audit they ran, show you an eval set from a past deployment, explain what the first version got wrong, and name the business metric a deployment moved. If they cannot answer at least three of those with specifics, they have not done the job before.

faqs.question: Is a forward deployed engineer full-time, contract, or embedded through a vendor?
faqs.answer: All three exist under the label. Some companies hire FDEs directly as full-time staff, some run project-based outcome engagements, and some use an embedded placement model where the engineer works inside the client's team without being a direct employee. None of these is more legitimate than the others; the structure should match how long the problem needs sustained attention.

faqs.question: Do I need a forward deployed engineer or a consultant?
faqs.answer:
Hire a consultant when you need an outside opinion, a feasibility study, or a roadmap before committing engineering time. Hire an FDE when the plan is clear enough and what you actually need is someone to build, ship, and own the result.

faqs.question: What does AI-native mean for a team?
faqs.answer: An AI-native team has restructured its workflows, conventions, and culture so that AI is a default participant in every process. It goes beyond having AI tool subscriptions. AI-native means the team has shared context files, documented AI-first workflows, and measures AI's impact on outcomes like shipping speed and code quality.

faqs.question: How long does it take to make a team AI-native?
faqs.answer: Most teams can complete the foundational transformation in 90 days. The 30-day onboarding program builds individual skills, and the following 60 days are spent refining shared workflows, building the prompt library, and establishing the measurement cadence. Full cultural adoption typically takes 6-12 months.

faqs.question: What is the best AI tool for team collaboration in 2026?
faqs.answer: For engineering-heavy teams, Claude with Claude Code offers the strongest team collaboration features, including CLAUDE.md shared context files, agent teams for parallel task execution, and a 1M-token context window. For Google Workspace-native organizations, Gemini integrates most cleanly. ChatGPT offers the broadest general-purpose capabilities and the largest plugin ecosystem.

faqs.question: How do you measure AI adoption success?
faqs.answer: Track outcome-based KPIs rather than usage metrics. The most important indicators are: time-to-first-draft reduction (target 40-50%), code review cycle time reduction (target 30%), deployment frequency increase (target 2x), and defect rate reduction (target 20%). Supplement these with a monthly employee satisfaction survey about AI tool usefulness.

faqs.question: Can non-technical teams become AI-native?
faqs.answer: Yes. The AI-native framework applies to any knowledge work team. Marketing teams use AI for content generation, research synthesis, and campaign analysis. Sales teams use AI for prospect research, email personalization, and CRM data enrichment. Operations teams use AI for process documentation, vendor analysis, and reporting. The key is the same: standardize on tools, build shared workflows, train systematically, and measure outcomes.

faqs.question: What is a CLAUDE.md file and why does it matter?
faqs.answer: A CLAUDE.md file is a project-level configuration document that gives Claude context about your codebase, conventions, and standards. It lives in the root of your repository and is automatically loaded when any team member uses Claude Code on that project. It matters because it ensures every team member gets consistent AI behavior regardless of their individual prompting skill, eliminating the "works for me but not for you" problem.

faqs.question: How much does it cost to make a team AI-native?
faqs.answer: Tool costs range from $20-30 per user per month for team plans on Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. The larger investment is time: expect 20-30 hours per team member during the 30-day onboarding period, plus 5-10 hours of leadership time to design workflows and run the audit. Most teams report a positive ROI within 60 days through time savings alone, with engineering teams seeing the fastest payback due to reduced code review cycles and faster shipping.

faqs.question: How do you handle team members who resist AI adoption?
faqs.answer:
Start by understanding the root cause. Resistance usually falls into three categories: lack of relevant training (they tried AI and it did not help with their specific tasks), legitimate concerns about quality or accuracy (which should be addressed with guardrails and review processes), or fear of job displacement (which requires honest conversation about how roles will evolve, not be eliminated). The most effective approach is pairing resistant team members with enthusiastic power users for the first two weeks. Seeing AI succeed on real work in their domain converts skeptics faster than any presentation.

/blog/how-to-sandbox-ai-agents-safely.title: How to Sandbox AI Agents Safely
/blog/how-to-sandbox-ai-agents-safely.description: An OpenAI eval agent broke its sandbox and breached Hugging Face. The practical playbook for scoped permissions, egress control, and approval gates so your agents cannot do the same.

faqs.question: What does it mean to sandbox an AI agent?
faqs.answer: Sandboxing an AI agent means running it inside an isolated environment with explicitly limited permissions, network access, and credentials, so that even if the agent tries to do something outside its intended task, it physically cannot reach anything beyond the boundary you set. A sandbox that still has open internet access or a shared long-lived credential is not actually isolated, which is the exact gap that let an OpenAI evaluation agent reach Hugging Face's production infrastructure in July 2026.

faqs.question: How do I control network egress for an AI agent?
faqs.answer: Put the agent's runtime behind an explicit allowlist of destinations it is permitted to reach, with the default set to block everything else. Log every attempted outbound call, including blocked ones, since a blocked call to an unexpected address is often the first sign something is wrong.

faqs.question: What is least-privilege access for AI agents?
faqs.answer: Least privilege means giving an agent only the specific permissions its current task requires, rather than the full access available on whatever account or platform it runs under. Build the permission set by starting from zero and adding only what the task needs, instead of starting broad and planning to narrow it later.

faqs.question: Why do AI agents need human approval gates?
faqs.answer: Human or policy approval gates stop an agent before it takes an action it cannot undo, such as deleting data, sending external messages, or changing a permission. Both the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident and a separate case involving an unattended agent used against a government finance ministry trace back to a removed or bypassed approval checkpoint, not a smarter attack.

faqs.question: Should test and evaluation environments be treated as production systems?
faqs.answer: Yes. The OpenAI evaluation environment involved in the Hugging Face breach was intended to be isolated and was not fully cut off from the internet in practice, which is what allowed an agent to escape it. Test isolation should be actively verified by attempting to reach the outside from inside the environment, not assumed from a configuration file.

faqs.question: What is agent observability and why does it matter?
faqs.answer: Agent observability means logging every tool call, credential use, and network destination an agent touches, with alerts on anomalous patterns like unexpected privilege escalation or unfamiliar outbound destinations. Hugging Face detected its own breach and reported it to law enforcement before OpenAI traced the activity back to its own eval, which was possible because Hugging Face had visibility into its own infrastructure.

faqs.question: Can a well-aligned AI model still cause a security incident?
faqs.answer:
Yes. An agent does not need to be malicious or misaligned to cause damage, it only needs a strong enough goal and a gap in its containment. The OpenAI models involved in the Hugging Face incident were not attempting sabotage, they were optimizing for completing an evaluation task and used whatever access the environment allowed to get there.

faqs.question: Do I need an Anthropic API key if I have Claude Pro?
faqs.answer: No. Claude Pro and Max subscriptions cover Claude Code usage directly. For most solo developers, Pro is the cheaper path. For a tier-by-tier breakdown of rate limits and what happens when you hit them, see Claude Code rate limits 2026.

faqs.question: Can I use Claude Code without Node.js?
faqs.answer: Yes. Anthropic ships a standalone binary at claude.ai/install.sh (macOS and Linux). It is a single executable, no Node runtime required, and it is the install method Anthropic's docs recommend. The npm package installs the same binary and remains supported.

faqs.question: Does Claude Code work on Windows?
faqs.answer: Yes, natively and in WSL. Anthropic's setup docs support Windows 10 1809+ and Windows Server 2019+: run irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex in PowerShell or the install.cmd command in CMD, no Administrator rights needed. Git for Windows is optional; with it, Claude Code uses Git Bash for shell commands, and without it, it uses PowerShell. Pick WSL instead if your projects and tools already live in Linux.

faqs.question: How much does Claude Code cost in 2026?
faqs.answer: Two pricing models. Subscription: Pro at $20/month ($17/month billed annually) or Max from $100/month, per claude.com/pricing in October 2026. API: metered per token. Heavy users typically spend $50-500/month depending on model choice and prompt size. Bedrock/Vertex bills through your cloud account at similar rates. Switch with /model to control cost mid-session.

faqs.question: What is the difference between CLAUDE.md and a system prompt?
faqs.answer: CLAUDE.md is project memory: it loads at every session start from your repo and stays in context. A system prompt is set once at the API level and applies to all conversations. For Claude Code specifically, you write CLAUDE.md, you do not write a system prompt. The CLI handles the system prompt for you.

faqs.question: Should I commit .claude/ to git?
faqs.answer: Yes for settings.json, agents/, and any project-level MCP config. No for transient files (sessions, caches). Those go in .gitignore. Sharing .claude/ is how your team gets the same defaults, sub-agents, and hooks without each developer setting it up manually.

faqs.question: Can I run multiple Claude Code sessions at once?
faqs.answer: Yes. Each terminal window is an independent session. Sub-agents run in their own context inside a session. Many teams run two or three sessions in parallel: one for the main feature, one for tests, one for docs. Tile them in your terminal multiplexer.

faqs.question: How do I update Claude Code?
faqs.answer:
Run claude update, or npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code@latest for an npm install (the docs advise against npm update -g). Anthropic ships updates roughly weekly in 2026. The CLI will tell you on launch if there is a new version. Native installs auto-update in the background by default (Homebrew and WinGet installs do not). To turn the background updater off for version-pinned environments, set "DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER": "1" in the env block of settings.json; DISABLE_UPDATES also blocks manual updates.

/blog/how-to-use-buzz-by-block.title: How to Use Buzz by Block: Agents as Team Members
/blog/how-to-use-buzz-by-block.description: Buzz is Jack Dorsey and Block's open-source workspace where AI agents join channels as real members behind one cryptographic identity system. Here is what works today, what's still coming, and how to set it up.

faqs.question: Is Buzz free?
faqs.answer: The desktop app and the open-source relay software are free. Block also runs a hosted relay option, still early and rough around the launch, so teams that do not want to run their own infrastructure can create a workspace without self-hosting.

faqs.question: Is Buzz the same as Slack?
faqs.answer: No. Buzz looks similar on the surface (channels, threads, DMs, search), but the underlying model is different: every message and every agent action is a signed cryptographic event stored on a relay you can host yourself, rather than data living inside one company's servers. Slack treats a bot as a plugin; Buzz gives an agent its own identity and its own audit trail as a workspace member.

faqs.question: Do I need to self-host?
faqs.answer: No, but it is worth considering. The desktop app pointed at Block's hosted relay is the fastest way to try Buzz. Self-hosting your own relay gives you control over where messages are stored and avoids relying on a third party's moderation policy for message privacy, and it was also the more stable path in the first weeks after launch while the hosted option worked through early traffic and onboarding issues.

faqs.question: What models and agents does Buzz support?
faqs.answer: Buzz is model-agnostic. It ships with harnesses for goose (Block's own open-source agent framework), Codex, and Claude Code, and each agent you create can be assigned its own harness and model independently of your workspace default.

faqs.question: Is my data private on Buzz?
faqs.answer: It depends on how you host it. On a self-hosted relay, you control the data and the retention policy entirely. On Block's hosted relay, messages are not end-to-end encrypted, and Block's own terms permit reading them for moderation or legal reasons. Teams with strict privacy requirements should self-host.

faqs.question: Does Buzz replace GitHub?
faqs.answer: Not yet, and Block is not claiming it fully does. The vision is git hosting built into the same relay, so a feature branch is a channel and a merge decision lives next to the conversation that led to it. That capability is being actively built, not finished, so most teams will run Buzz alongside their existing code host for now rather than migrating off it immediately.

faqs.question: Can Buzz agents talk to each other on their own?
faqs.answer: Only when tagged. Agents in Buzz respond to @ mentions rather than reacting to every message in a channel, which keeps multi-agent channels from turning into constant noise. If you deliberately set up agents that mention each other, write an explicit stopping condition into their instructions, since Buzz's routing does not enforce one for you automatically.

faqs.question: What is the single biggest catch right now?
faqs.answer:
Buzz is early. Version numbers are still in the 0.4.x range, mobile apps are not out yet, full git hosting and approval gates are unfinished, and the first days after launch saw real onboarding friction on the hosted relay. The core idea, agents as identified, auditable workspace members, works today. The parts that would make it a complete Slack-and-GitHub replacement are still being built.

/blog/how-to-use-jev-guide.title: How to Use Jev: A Tested Step-by-Step Guide With Working Code (2026)
/blog/how-to-use-jev-guide.description: A practical guide to TypeSafe Jev where every request was run against the live API. Setup, the three question types, eight recipes with curl, Python and JavaScript, decision-policy tables, cost math, error handling, a production checklist and when not to use it.

faqs.question: What is Jev?
faqs.answer: Jev is TypeSafe's flagship System One model. It takes state and typed questions and returns probabilities and a confidence value in a fixed schema, instead of generated text.

faqs.question: How much does Jev cost?
faqs.answer: The docs list $0.042 per million input tokens, with output tokens free. Our measured cost was $0.0151 per 1,000 decisions on 8-way intent routing.

faqs.question: Do I need the SDK?
faqs.answer: No. The API is one POST endpoint, and every example here uses plain HTTP. The Python SDK is typesafe-sdk and the JavaScript SDK is @typesafe-ai/sdk, and both add retries.

faqs.question: Which model id should I send?
faqs.answer: Send jev-latest while you experiment. For production, send a version id such as jev-1.13.0 so results do not shift under you, and log the model field from each response.

faqs.question: What is the difference between probabilities and confidence?
faqs.answer: Probabilities are the full distribution over your options or levels. Confidence is a single number derived from that distribution. For three options the docs give the formula (3 times the largest probability, minus 1) divided by 2, so an even split scores 0 and a clear winner scores 1.

faqs.question: Does a noul have a confidence?
faqs.answer: No. A noul returns one probability between 0 and 1. Gate on cutoffs you set from labeled data.

faqs.question: What confidence threshold should I use?
faqs.answer: The docs suggest acting automatically above 0.9, confirming in the middle and not acting below 0.5, with higher thresholds for higher stakes. Ours: at 0.90 or more, Jev was right 95.5 percent of the time on 8-way intent, but not every time.

faqs.question: How many options can a choice have?
faqs.answer: Up to 255. A score takes 2 to 10 levels.

faqs.question: Can I ask many questions at once?
faqs.answer: Yes, and you should. TypeSafe's cookbook measured identical answers, 12.2 times lower cost and a 10 times speedup for 13 questions in one call. The docs do not state a hard cap on question count.

faqs.question: How fast is it?
faqs.answer: In our test, median latency was 0.33 seconds and 95th percentile was 0.44 seconds across 791 calls through OpenRouter. The slowest single call took 1.42 seconds.

faqs.question: Is Jev more accurate than GPT or Claude?
faqs.answer: Not in our test. It was level with the small models and behind GPT-5.6 Terra on intent routing. It was much cheaper and faster, and its confidence score supported a cascade that matched Terra's accuracy at about 26 to 28 percent of the cost.

faqs.question: Can Jev read images or PDFs?
faqs.answer: Not directly. Input is text only. Extract the text first, then pass it as state.

faqs.question: What are the rate limits?
faqs.answer: The Models page lists 250,000 tokens per second and 1,200 requests per minute. Exceeding either returns 429.

faqs.question: Can it write text or code?
faqs.answer: No. The docs say it is not trained to generate text. Pair it with a normal LLM when you need prose, and use Jev to decide what to do with it.

/blog/human-in-the-loop-ai-automation.title: Human-in-the-Loop AI Automation: Where to Put the Checkpoint (2026)
/blog/human-in-the-loop-ai-automation.description: The main human-in-the-loop models (pre-execution approval, post-execution review, confidence-based routing, exception-only escalation) and how to decide where the checkpoint belongs.

faqs.question: What is human-in-the-loop AI automation?
faqs.answer: Human-in-the-loop AI automation is a design pattern where specific points in an otherwise automated workflow route through a person for approval, correction, or review, chosen deliberately based on the risk and reversibility of the action rather than applied uniformly.

faqs.question: Is human-in-the-loop the opposite of full automation?
faqs.answer: No, it's a spectrum, not a binary. Most production systems combine autonomous execution for low-stakes, reversible actions with human checkpoints reserved for higher-stakes or harder-to-reverse decisions, rather than choosing one extreme.

faqs.question: What's the difference between pre-execution approval and post-execution review?
faqs.answer: Pre-execution approval blocks an action until a person approves it, preventing a mistake from happening but adding latency to every action. Post-execution review lets the action complete and has a person check it afterward, preserving speed but only catching mistakes after they've already occurred.

faqs.question: How do I decide which actions need a human checkpoint?
faqs.answer: Start with reversibility: irreversible or hard-to-undo actions are stronger candidates for pre-execution approval, while reversible, low-stakes actions can usually run autonomously with post-execution review. Volume and blast radius matter too, a bulk action often deserves more scrutiny than the same action performed once.

faqs.question: Does adding more human checkpoints always make a system safer?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Over-applying approval gates on low-stakes actions increases latency and often leads to rubber-stamping rather than genuine review, which erodes both the safety benefit and the efficiency gain the automation was meant to provide.

faqs.question: How does human-in-the-loop relate to AI agent guardrails?
faqs.answer:
Human-in-the-loop checkpoints are one specific type of guardrail, focused on routing decisions through a person rather than enforcing a rule automatically. Both are part of the same broader discipline of constraining what an autonomous system can do without oversight.

For the broader safety design this connects to, see our guide to AI agent guardrails and AI agent security best practices. Our custom workflow automation service designs the human checkpoints into a workflow from the start, based on where the actual risk sits, not as a blanket default.

/blog/intelligent-document-processing-gu.description: A practitioner walkthrough of the IDP pipeline: OCR and layout recognition, field extraction, validation, and routing, plus what Textract, Azure AI Document Intelligence, and LlamaParse are each actually good at.

faqs.question: What's the difference between OCR and intelligent document processing?
faqs.answer: OCR is one stage inside IDP, specifically the step that converts an image into recognized text and layout. IDP is the full pipeline: OCR, then extraction of specific fields, then validation of those fields, then routing the result to the right destination. A tool that only does OCR hands you text; an IDP pipeline hands you structured, validated data ready for a downstream system.

faqs.question: Can intelligent document processing handle handwritten documents accurately?
faqs.answer: Less reliably than printed or typed text, across every major tool (Textract, Azure AI Document Intelligence, Google Document AI all included). Handwriting recognition has improved but still lags printed-text recognition meaningfully, so document types with significant handwritten content should route a larger share to human review by design, not as an exception.

faqs.question: Do I need machine learning expertise to set up an IDP pipeline?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Managed services like Textract, Azure AI Document Intelligence, and Google Document AI expose prebuilt models through an API call, no model training required for common document types (invoices, receipts, IDs, general forms). Custom model training or building a validation and routing layer around the extraction API is where engineering effort is genuinely needed, and that's usually the bulk of the actual implementation work.

faqs.question: How accurate is AI-based document extraction compared to manual data entry?
faqs.answer: It depends heavily on document quality and type, which is exactly why the answer isn't a single number worth quoting without context. On clean, typed documents of a well-represented type (a standard invoice format, a typed form), extraction accuracy is generally strong. On poor scans, unusual layouts, or handwritten content, accuracy drops meaningfully and the review rate should rise accordingly. The right way to know your actual accuracy is testing against your own real document mix, not relying on a vendor's benchmark numbers from a curated dataset.

faqs.question: What happens to documents that fail extraction or validation?
faqs.answer: In a properly built pipeline, they get routed to a human review queue with the specific flagged fields highlighted, not dumped back to square one for a full manual re-entry. Documents that can't even be classified or read (corrupted files, unsupported formats, unrecognized document types) should go to a separate exception queue rather than being force-processed through the wrong extraction path, which is how bad data ends up silently downstream.

faqs.question: Is LlamaParse a replacement for Textract or Azure Document Intelligence?
faqs.answer:
Not directly, they solve overlapping but different problems. LlamaParse is built to turn complex documents into clean, structured text (often markdown) for feeding into LLM-based workflows and RAG pipelines. Textract and Azure AI Document Intelligence are built as full extraction services with normalized field output, per-field confidence scores, and prebuilt models for specific document types like invoices and IDs. A pipeline needing guaranteed schema compliance and confidence-based validation typically still relies on Textract or Azure Document Intelligence for the extraction stage, even if LlamaParse or a similar tool is used elsewhere for LLM-facing document parsing.

If you're evaluating vendor options rather than building a custom pipeline, see our roundup of document automation software. Our custom automation service builds document-processing pipelines with the validation and routing stages built in from the start, not bolted on after accuracy problems show up in production.

/blog/invoice-automation-ai.description: What AI invoice automation actually does (extraction, three-way matching, anomaly detection), where a human still needs to be involved, and how to evaluate a system.

faqs.question: What is AI invoice automation?
faqs.answer: AI invoice automation is a system that extracts structured data from incoming invoices, matches it against purchase orders and existing records, and routes invoices through an approval workflow, using AI-based extraction that adapts to varied invoice formats rather than requiring a fixed template per vendor.

faqs.question: Does AI invoice automation replace accounts payable staff?
faqs.answer: It replaces the manual data entry and routine matching work, letting staff focus on genuine discrepancies, vendor relationship issues, and final payment decisions rather than keying in every invoice by hand.

faqs.question: How accurate is AI-based invoice data extraction?
faqs.answer: Accuracy varies with document quality and format complexity, and generally improves with a system's exposure to a specific vendor's typical invoice layout. Testing on your own actual vendor mix, rather than a generic demo set, is the practical way to validate accuracy before rolling it out.

faqs.question: What happens when an AI invoice automation system isn't confident in an extraction?
faqs.answer: A well-designed system flags low-confidence extractions for human review rather than passing an uncertain guess through automatically, since an undetected wrong amount or vendor match is one of the more costly failure modes in accounts payable automation.

faqs.question: Should every invoice go through the same level of automated processing?
faqs.answer: No. New or unverified vendor relationships and invoices with genuine discrepancies against a purchase order should route to human review, while well-matched invoices from established vendors are reasonable candidates for more automated handling.

faqs.question: Does invoice automation remove the need for human approval on payments?
faqs.answer:
No. Automating extraction, matching, and routing streamlines the process leading up to payment, but final authorization, particularly for larger amounts, should still involve human sign-off as part of standard financial controls.

For the broader decision framework on where automation should stop and a human checkpoint belongs, see human-in-the-loop AI automation. /blog/jev-pricing-cost-per-decision.title: Jev Pricing (2026): What It Costs Per Decision, and Is It Free?
/blog/jev-pricing-cost-per-decision.description: Jev costs $0.042 per million input tokens with free output. Measured cost per 1,000 decisions against GPT, Claude and Gemini, where it is free until September 25, and how to estimate your own bill.

faqs.question: How much does Jev cost?
faqs.answer: TypeSafe lists $0.042 per million input tokens with free output, which is $42 per billion input tokens. In our test, 1,000 short routing decisions cost about 1.5 cents.

faqs.question: Is Jev free?
faqs.answer: No. Vercel's AI Gateway offered Jev free until September 25, 2026, and that window has ended. As of October 23, 2026, TypeSafe and Vercel's AI Gateway list Jev at $0.042 per million input tokens, with output free. Check the provider's page for the current terms.

faqs.question: Why is output free?
faqs.answer: Jev returns typed answers with probabilities and does not generate text, so there are no output tokens to bill. You still pay for the input, which includes your questions.

faqs.question: How do I estimate my monthly Jev bill?
faqs.answer: Multiply your monthly request count by the average input tokens per request, divide by one million, and multiply by $0.042. Measure the token count from a few real requests, because the questions count, not just the state.

faqs.question: Is Jev cheaper than GPT or Claude?
faqs.answer: For short bounded decisions, yes. In our test it was 4.7 to 7.5 times cheaper than the two cheapest small models and 40 to 49 times cheaper than GPT-5.6 Terra per decision. It is not a replacement for a large model on writing or reasoning.

faqs.question: Does asking more questions cost more?
faqs.answer: Yes, by the tokens in the extra questions. It does not cost a full extra request, because the state is read once and all questions are answered together.

faqs.question: Is there still a free Jev window?
faqs.answer: Not that we could find on October 23, 2026. The Vercel AI Gateway window ended on September 25, 2026, and you now pay the per-token price through whichever provider you use. If you built during the free window, price your workload at $0.042 per million input tokens.

faqs.question: How can I keep Jev costs low?
faqs.answer:
Batch questions over the same state, keep question criteria short, cap retries, and use a confidence gate so only uncertain items go to a larger model.

/blog/jev-typesafe-system-one-model.description: TypeSafe AI came out of stealth Sept 15, 2026 with $40M in funding and Jev, a model that returns typed decisions instead of generated text. Three days later it's listed on OpenRouter, and developers report wiring it into Claude Code, browser automation, and ad analysis.

faqs.question: What is TypeSafe AI's Jev?
faqs.answer: Jev is the first "System One" model from TypeSafe AI, a startup founded by former OpenAI researcher Diogo Almeida. Instead of generating text, it takes an application's state and a typed question and returns a calibrated probability for a predefined set of answers (a choice, a yes/no, or a position on a scale).

faqs.question: When was Jev released?
faqs.answer: TypeSafe AI came out of stealth with Jev and $40 million in seed funding on September 15, 2026. OpenRouter added Jev Latest and Jev 1.13 on September 18, 2026, which is when a wider wave of developer builds and public reactions followed.

faqs.question: How much does Jev cost?
faqs.answer: TypeSafe states $0.042 per million input tokens, with output tokens free since Jev returns a typed decision rather than generated text. That figure is the vendor's own stated price, confirmed on TypeSafe's homepage at time of writing.

faqs.question: Is Jev a replacement for Claude Code or ChatGPT?
faqs.answer: No. Jev doesn't generate text, hold a conversation, or write code. Early builds use it alongside an existing agent or chat model, handling the narrow classification, routing, and verification decisions inside a workflow while the chat model or coding agent still does the parts that require generation or open-ended reasoning.

faqs.question: How do I get access to Jev?
faqs.answer: As of October 23, 2026, TypeSafe's quick start says to get an API key from the TypeSafe console (console.typesafe.ai), and also offers SDKs, an agent skill and a browser Playground. Jev is also on Vercel's AI Gateway and on OpenRouter, which serves it through a separate decisions endpoint rather than the usual chat completions endpoint. Our how to use Jev guide walks through the first request.

faqs.question: What is TypeSafe AI's pricing?
faqs.answer: TypeSafe prices Jev at $42 per billion input tokens ($0.042 per million), and output tokens are free. Jev 1.14 and Jev 1.13 list the same price on TypeSafe's models page.

faqs.question: What is a "System One" model?
faqs.answer:
The term references Daniel Kahneman's distinction between fast, intuitive System 1 thinking and slower, deliberate System 2 thinking. TypeSafe uses it to describe a model category built for fast, structured decisions software can act on directly, as distinct from the slower, generative, conversational category most current LLMs fall into.

Sources: TypeSafe AI's site and documentation (docs.typesafe.ai), OpenRouter's TypeSafe page, TechCrunch, The Register, InfoWorld, TechStock2 and Forkast, plus public X posts from developers, checked September 18 and 19, 2026. Almeida's background is as described by DCVC and the press coverage above.

faqs.question: How fast is Jev?
faqs.answer: TypeSafe's launch material puts response time in the tens to hundreds of milliseconds. In our own test through OpenRouter, median latency was 0.33 seconds, and the slowest of 791 calls took 1.42 seconds. Measure it from your own environment before you rely on it.

faqs.question: What can Jev not do?
faqs.answer: It does not write text, it does not read images, and its input is limited: per TypeSafe's docs, the state plus all questions in one request has a 64k token budget. It is built for bounded decisions, so use a larger model for writing, long reasoning and open-ended tasks.

faqs.question: Where can I see what people built with Jev?

In our index of Jev use cases and examples, which lists more than 1,300 public builds, demos and tests, each scored by Jev for how specific and checkable it is.

faqs.question: What is Jev used for?
faqs.answer: Jev is used for structured decisions inside software, such as routing tickets, checking LLM tool calls, reranking search results and scoring items against a rubric. It answers with a choice, a score or a yes/no probability plus a confidence value, not text.

faqs.question: What are the main Jev use cases?
faqs.answer: TypeSafe's docs group them into AI automation software, real-time applications, big-data map-reduce, universal verification and harness engineering. Industry examples include customer support, recruiting, insurance claims, financial crime, marketplaces and moderation.

faqs.question: Can Jev replace an LLM?
faqs.answer: Not for generation. It fits the narrow decisions around an LLM, and the analysts InfoWorld quotes expect the two to sit side by side. The Vercel and Bryo AI reports in TechCrunch show cases where it replaced or competed with an LLM on a single classification task.

faqs.question: How do I get access to Jev?
faqs.answer: As of September 19, 2026, TypeSafe runs a waitlist, per InfoWorld and TechStock2. OpenRouter also lists "Jev Latest" and "Jev 1.13" on its TypeSafe page.

faqs.question: Are the speed and cost numbers reliable?
faqs.answer: Treat them as vendor-reported. TechStock2 says TypeSafe's own team built the benchmark and scored against two external models rather than a ground-truth key. Test on your own data.

faqs.question: Does Jev explain its decisions?
faqs.answer:
No. It returns a probability, not a reason. If you need explanations, log the inputs, answers and thresholds for every call, or use a model that can produce a rationale.

Related: Jev and TypeSafe's System One model, explained

faqs.question: Where can I find real Jev examples and case studies?
faqs.answer: The Jev builds index lists more than 1,300 public builds, demos and tests from X, LinkedIn and GitHub, sorted by use case. These are community projects and the numbers are each builder's own claims. We have not used Jev on client work yet.

faqs.question: How much does Jev cost?
faqs.answer: TypeSafe lists $0.042 per million input tokens with free output. Vercel Developers announced free access to Jev on its AI Gateway until September 25, 2026. Prices and free windows change, so check the model page before you build on it.

faqs.question: Can Jev run locally?
faqs.answer: Not the official model. TypeSafe serves Jev through its API and through providers such as Vercel AI Gateway. Community projects imitate the same interface with open models on a local machine, for example a local stand-in built on omlx and a semantic if-statement library for a home GPU, but those are not Jev and their accuracy is their own. Both are listed in our index of Jev builds.

faqs.question: Is Jev open source?
faqs.answer: We found no released model weights in launch week, so plan on using it through an API. Check TypeSafe's documentation for the current position before you design around either answer.

faqs.question: What are the three Jev question types?
faqs.answer: Choice picks one option from a set you define and returns a probability for every option. Score rates the state on an ordered scale and can land between two levels. Noul answers a yes or no question as a probability. You can put many questions of any type in one request.

faqs.question: How fast is Jev?
faqs.answer: TypeSafe's launch material puts response time in the tens to hundreds of milliseconds. In our own test through OpenRouter, median latency was 0.33 seconds, with the slowest of 791 calls at 1.42 seconds. Latency depends on your network path, so measure it from your own environment.

faqs.question: What is a confidence gate?
faqs.answer:
A rule that acts on Jev's answer only when its confidence is high enough, and sends the rest to a larger model or a person. In our test, keeping only answers at 0.90 confidence or higher lifted accuracy on an 8-way routing task from 83.8 percent to 95.5 percent, while answering 70 percent of the items.

faqs.question: How much cheaper is Claude Haiku 5.5 than Haiku 4.5 in practice?
faqs.answer: In our test, 7.1 to 7.7 times cheaper per decision. The list price is 10 times lower ($0.10/$0.50 against $1/$5 per million tokens), but Haiku 5.5's tokenizer counted 34 to 39 percent more input tokens for the same prompts, and it billed a few more output tokens per answer.

faqs.question: Is Claude Haiku 5.5 cheaper than Jev?
faqs.answer: No. Jev was 3.3 to 4.4 times cheaper per decision than Haiku 5.5 on our three tasks: $0.0151 against $0.0500 per 1,000 decisions on 8-way intent routing.

faqs.question: Is Claude Haiku 5.5 faster than Jev?
faqs.answer: No. Haiku 5.5's median latency was 1.36 seconds against 0.36 seconds for Jev in the same run, and Jev's slowest call (1.21 s) was faster than Haiku 5.5's median.

faqs.question: Is Claude Haiku 5.5 more accurate than Haiku 4.5?
faqs.answer: Not across the board. It scored higher on 8-way intent routing (83.8% vs 78.8%, not significant), about the same on 77-way routing, and significantly lower on prompt-injection detection (84.8% vs 89.0%, p = 0.008).

faqs.question: How does Claude Sonnet 5.5 compare with Jev?
faqs.answer: Sonnet 5.5 was more accurate on 8-way routing (90.0% vs 84.4%) and injection detection (90.8% vs 87.0%), tied on 77-way routing, and cost 64 to 88 times more per decision. Jev in front of Sonnet 5.5 at a 0.80 confidence gate came within 0.6 points of Sonnet's accuracy for 22 to 24 percent of its cost.

faqs.question: What is the cheapest LLM for classification?
faqs.answer:
Of the Claude models we tested, Haiku 5.5, at about $0.05 per 1,000 short decisions. Jev, a decision model rather than a chat LLM, was cheaper still at about $0.015. In our September run, GPT-5.4 nano ($0.070) and Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite ($0.087) sat between the two on the same task, but they were measured on a different day.

faqs.question: Is Jev faster than GPT-5.6 Terra?

faqs.question: Do the 193.6x and 444.6x claims hold up?

faqs.question: What is Kimi K3.1 Pro?
faqs.answer: Kimi K3.1 Pro is Moonshot AI's flagship large language model, released on October 23, 2026. faqs.question: How much does Kimi K3.1 Pro cost?
faqs.answer: On the Kimi API it costs $2 per million input tokens, $10 per million output tokens and $0.20 per million cached input tokens. The Highspeed variant costs $4 / $20 with the same $0.20 cached-input price. Access requires a top-up of at least $1.

faqs.question: When will Kimi K3.1 Pro be open weights?
faqs.answer: Moonshot says "by Nov 4, 2026." As of October 25, 2026 the weights were not yet published and no license had been announced. The open release has cyber-related training data removed.

faqs.question: Is Kimi K3.1 Pro better than Claude Opus 5.5?
faqs.answer: Not on independent testing. Artificial Analysis scores Opus 5.5 at 58 and K3.1 Pro at 55. Moonshot's own Terminal-Bench 4.0 result puts them within a point (65.7% vs 66.4%). K3.1 Pro costs half as much per token.

faqs.question: What is the difference between Kimi K3.1 Pro and Highspeed?

faqs.question: Can you turn off reasoning in Kimi K3.1 Pro?

faqs.question: What is the context window of Kimi K3.1 Pro?

/blog/legacy-system-migration-ai.description: Where AI genuinely helps in a legacy migration (understanding undocumented code, drafting translations, test generation), and where it falls short of real validation.

faqs.question: How does AI help with legacy system migration?
faqs.answer: AI accelerates understanding of undocumented legacy code, surfaces hidden dependencies and edge cases, generates first-draft translations to a modern language or framework, and creates test baselines from observed behavior, all speeding up the analysis and drafting phases of a migration.

faqs.question: Can AI fully automate a legacy system migration?
faqs.answer: No. Validating that migrated behavior is actually correct, understanding business context not reflected in the code, and making architecture decisions for the new system all require human judgment that AI-assisted analysis supports but doesn't replace.

faqs.question: How do I validate that a migrated system behaves the same as the legacy one?
faqs.answer: Generate tests that capture the legacy system's actual observed behavior before migration begins, creating a concrete baseline the new system can be validated against, rather than relying on potentially outdated documentation of intended behavior.

faqs.question: What's the biggest risk in an AI-assisted legacy migration?
faqs.answer: Treating an AI-generated translation as correct without full review and validation against a behavioral baseline. A plausible-looking translation isn't the same as a verified-correct one, and skipping that verification is where migration bugs most often originate.

faqs.question: Can AI recover tribal knowledge about a legacy system?
faqs.answer: No. Tribal knowledge that was never captured in code comments or documentation isn't recoverable through code analysis alone, which means budgeting time for conversations with people who understand the system's history remains a necessary part of the migration.

faqs.question: Should AI-assisted migration replace a full manual code review of the new system?
faqs.answer:
No. AI-generated translations should go through the same review rigor as any code change, checked against a behavioral test baseline and reviewed by an engineer, not deployed based on the AI system's output alone.

faqs.answer: Yes. n8n ships a dedicated AI Agent node with native LangChain integration, letting you build tool-using, multi-step AI agents inside a workflow rather than as a separate product. This is the clearest technical differentiator between n8n and Make or Zapier as of 2026.

faqs.question: Does Zapier have AI features?
faqs.answer: Yes. Since October 2026, Zapier Agents runs as a single AI by Zapier step inside the Zap editor, and AI steps bill as tasks on the same plan as your other Zaps: default models are free, other model tiers cost 1, 3 or 5 tasks per step (Zapier's announcement). A run that crosses 75 tasks pauses for a person. Existing agents are not moved for you; each one is recreated as an AI step.

faqs.question: Is n8n harder to use than Zapier or Make?
faqs.answer: Generally, yes. n8n has the steepest learning curve of the three, especially if you self-host, since teams without a developer on staff often spend meaningful time managing the underlying infrastructure. Zapier is built for the least technical setup, and Make sits in between, offering more visual logic control than Zapier without n8n's infrastructure overhead.

faqs.question: Which platform has the most app integrations?
faqs.answer: Zapier has the widest app coverage of the three, connecting to more than 7,000 apps as of 2026. Make connects to more than 3,000 apps, and n8n ships 400 or more official nodes plus a broader community-contributed catalog, with the option to build custom nodes for anything not natively supported.

faqs.question: Should I hire an agency instead of building workflows myself on one of these platforms?
faqs.answer: If you have one or two simple automations, building them yourself on any of these three platforms is reasonable. Once you need several AI-driven workflows built with proper error handling, monitoring, and someone accountable for fixing failures after launch, a dedicated n8n development agency or automation partner closes a gap that platform choice alone does not solve.

faqs.question: Is n8n's rising valuation a sign it is the safer long-term choice?
faqs.answer:
n8n's valuation reportedly doubled to $5.2 billion in May 2026 following a strategic investment from SAP, after a $180 million Series C in October 2025 at a $2.5 billion valuation. That level of investment is a meaningful signal of enterprise confidence and long-term platform viability, though valuation alone does not determine which tool is the right technical fit for your specific workflow.

faqs.question: What does MCP certification mean?
faqs.answer: MCP certification, specifically the MCPA (Model Context Protocol Associate), means a candidate passed a proctored exam demonstrating they understand MCP's architecture, message flow, security model, and real-world implementation patterns. It is issued by the Agentic AI Foundation, the Linux Foundation project that maintains MCP itself.

faqs.question: How much does the MCP certification cost?
faqs.answer: The MCPA exam costs $250 for a single attempt with one included retake. A 20% discount ($200) is available when purchased through AAIF conference registration (AGNTCon + MCPCon Europe or North America).

faqs.question: Is there an official MCP certification course?
faqs.answer: No, not as of this certification's September 2026 launch. The Linux Foundation offers only the exam plus free reference resources (the MCP spec, AAIF project pages, community blog posts). Third-party "MCP courses" that existed before the MCPA are unrelated training products, not official exam prep.

faqs.question: How long is the MCPA exam?
faqs.answer: Sources conflict. The AAIF launch press release states 120 minutes; the Linux Foundation's own MCPA certification page lists 90 minutes in its spec sheet. Until this is reconciled, prepare for the longer stated duration.

faqs.question: What are the prerequisites for MCPA?
faqs.answer: There are no mandatory prerequisites, but the Linux Foundation recommends familiarity with JSON-RPC or similar protocols, experience calling LLM APIs, understanding of agentic AI patterns like ReAct and tool use, basic security concepts (API keys, OAuth 2.1), and the ability to read MCP server manifests.

faqs.question: Who should get MCP certified?
faqs.answer: Engineers building or maintaining MCP servers, platform teams standardizing on MCP, AI governance and security reviewers, and consultants or agencies delivering MCP integrations to clients. It is not designed for general AI users or people whose only MCP exposure is a consumer chat app's tool settings.

faqs.question: Is MCPA a good certification to pursue right now?
faqs.answer: The protocol adoption behind it is real and well documented, and the exam content maps to genuine production concerns rather than trivia. But the certification itself is one week old at time of writing, with no track record on whether employers will actually filter for it. Treat "is it worth it" as an open question rather than a settled one for now.

faqs.question: How long is the MCPA certification valid?
faqs.answer:
Once earned, the credential is valid for 2 years. Candidates have 12 months from purchase to sit the exam itself.

/blog/mcp-security.title: MCP Security: What to Check Before You Connect a Server (2026)
/blog/mcp-security.description: The real attack surface MCP introduces: tool description poisoning, over-privileged servers, and unvetted third-party connections. Includes a verified walkthrough of the Supabase MCP prompt-injection demonstration and a scoping checklist.

faqs.question: What is MCP security?
faqs.answer: MCP security is the set of practices that control what a Model Context Protocol server can access and do once an AI agent connects to it, covering credential scoping, tool description review, and treating server-fetched data as untrusted input rather than instructions.

faqs.question: What is a Tool Poisoning Attack?
faqs.answer: A Tool Poisoning Attack is a technique, disclosed by Invariant Labs in April 2025, where a malicious MCP server embeds hidden instructions inside a tool's description field. The AI model reads the full description, but the user's interface typically shows only a simplified summary, so the user never sees the hidden instruction that manipulates the model's behavior.

faqs.question: Did Supabase's MCP server actually leak customer data?
faqs.answer: No confirmed customer breach has been reported. General Analysis ran a controlled July 2025 demonstration on a test project populated with dummy data, showing that a Supabase MCP connection using elevated service_role credentials could be manipulated through a prompt-injected support ticket into leaking a sensitive table's contents. Supabase's own documentation acknowledges this class of risk and recommends read-only mode and project scoping as mitigations.

faqs.question: How do I scope an MCP server's permissions?
faqs.answer: Connect it with the least-privileged credential the task allows, ideally read-only, restrict it to the specific database, project, or directory it needs rather than an entire account, and disable write or execute tool groups unless the workflow specifically requires them.

faqs.question: Are third-party MCP servers safe to use?
faqs.answer: Treat any third-party MCP server as an unreviewed dependency. Read its tool descriptions before connecting, check what data it can reach, and run it in a sandboxed environment where possible, especially for servers with filesystem or shell access.

faqs.question: What's the difference between MCP security and general AI agent security?
faqs.answer: MCP security is specifically about the server layer: what a connected server can access and what a malicious or compromised server can do to an agent. Broader AI agent security also covers how the agent itself handles autonomous execution, tool-use approval gates, and prompt injection from any untrusted source, not only MCP servers.

faqs.question: Is there a scanner for MCP server security?
faqs.answer: Yes. MCP-Scan, released by Invariant Labs in April 2025, checks connected MCP servers for known tool poisoning patterns and other risky configurations before you rely on them in production.

faqs.question: Should I let an AI coding agent connect its own MCP servers without review?
faqs.answer:
No. Every MCP server an agent connects to should go through the same review as a new dependency: read what it can access, confirm the credential it's using is scoped down, and log what it actually does once connected. If you want that review done systematically across your Claude Code or agent setup, our Claude Code security audit covers MCP server permissions, prompt injection exposure, and credential scoping as part of a full hardening pass.

If your team is connecting MCP servers to production data and wants a second set of eyes on what those servers can actually reach, book a consultation and we'll walk through your current setup before anything gets hardened.

faqs.question: What is an MCP server?
faqs.answer: An MCP server is a program that exposes your systems, APIs, databases, and tools to AI agents through the Model Context Protocol. It advertises tools the agent can call and resources the agent can read, over JSON-RPC, so any MCP-compatible client (Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot, and others) can use it.

faqs.question: When do I need a custom MCP server instead of an off-the-shelf one?
faqs.answer: You need a custom MCP server when the system you are connecting is proprietary, sensitive, or encodes business logic no public connector covers. Off-the-shelf servers are right for generic tools like web search or GitHub. Custom builds are right for internal CRMs, domain databases, private APIs, and regulated data where you must own the security boundary.

faqs.question: How long does it take to build a custom MCP server?
faqs.answer: A focused single-integration server typically takes a few weeks; production multi-tenant or regulated builds run longer. Published references cite around 12 weeks with multiple engineers for complex enterprise servers. Timeline is driven mostly by integration count, auth complexity, and compliance requirements rather than the protocol itself.

faqs.question: How much does MCP server development cost?
faqs.answer: Third-party 2026 pricing guides put basic custom servers near $9,000 to $40,000 in year one, SMB MVPs around $25,000 to $50,000, and production multi-tenant builds at $60,000 to $120,000 or more. Regulated builds can exceed $250,000, with compliance like HIPAA adding 30 to 40%. Cost scales with integrations, security, and scale, so treat ranges as signals, not quotes.

faqs.question: Is MCP secure enough for enterprise systems?
faqs.answer: MCP can be secure for enterprise use, but security depends entirely on how the server is built, not on the protocol alone. The risks are real because the server is an execution surface into live systems. Safe servers use least-privilege tool scoping, real authentication mapped to actual permissions, prompt-injection defenses, audit logging, and human approval for destructive actions.

faqs.question: Will a custom MCP server work with both Claude and ChatGPT?
faqs.answer: Yes. MCP is a vendor-neutral standard adopted by Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft and now governed under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation. A correctly built server works across MCP-compatible clients, so you build the integration once instead of maintaining a separate connector per AI vendor.

faqs.question: Can I build an MCP server myself with an AI coding assistant?
faqs.answer: You can scaffold a basic MCP server with an AI coding assistant, and many teams do. The gap is production safety: auth, least-privilege scoping, prompt-injection defense, and behavior under real agent traffic. A common and sensible path is to build a first version internally and then have it audited and hardened before it connects to production systems.

faqs.question: What is the difference between MCP tools, resources, and prompts?
faqs.answer:
Tools are functions the agent can invoke, like querying a database or creating a ticket. Resources are data the agent can read, like documents or records. Prompts are reusable templates that guide how the agent uses the server. Most custom servers rely mainly on tools and resources, with prompts used to standardize common workflows.
